intro:
This exposition proves the relative-entropy bound for Gaussian Unadjusted Langevin under a log-Sobolev inequality. The source result is Rapid Convergence of the Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm: Isoperimetry Suffices by Vempala and Wibisono (2019), Theorem 2. The theorem overview states the result and links to the individual proofs.

Assume that the potential is differentiable with Lipschitz gradient, its normalized Gibbs law satisfies the stated log-Sobolev inequality, the step satisfies the displayed restriction, and the initial relative entropy is finite. The proof constructs the positive-time Gaussian density, proves finite Fisher information and entropy, derives an integrated entropy identity using bounded logarithmic tests, and controls the initial time by a continuous entropy upper bound. The gradient moment estimate and the comparison between the log-Sobolev and smoothness constants are derived from these assumptions.

The first sections also state intermediate results under explicit density and regularity hypotheses. The subsequent Gaussian construction supplies the analytic estimates needed for the final theorem. Young’s inequality retains three quarters of the Fisher dissipation; scalar comparison and geometric summation give the coefficients \(6\) and \(8\).

sections.title: The entropy bound and its normalization
sections.intro:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, let \(n=\dim E\), and let \(\nu\) be the Gibbs probability measure associated with a differentiable potential \(U\). The potential has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. The assumed functional inequality is a log-Sobolev inequality for \(\nu\).

The source bound writes the dimension as \(d\); throughout these formulas \(d=n\).

steps.title: The ULA entropy estimate and its intermediate density hypotheses
steps.body:
For independent Gaussian ULA, \(X_{k+1}=X_k-h abla U(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}Z_k\), the final result is

\[0<h\le rac\alpha{4L^2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H_ u( ho_k)\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_ u( ho_0)+ rac{8hdL^2}{\alpha}.\]

The first term contracts the initial entropy; the second is the persistent discretization term. The bound follows from the target log-Sobolev inequality, differentiability, the Lipschitz gradient bound, and finite initial relative entropy. The intermediate result stated here assumes a relative-density path with the specified law, entropy regularity, entropy-production inequality, and gradient moment bound. The subsequent Gaussian analysis proves the corresponding properties from the original hypotheses. Thus the intermediate density assumptions are not extra hypotheses of the final ULA estimate.

steps.title: Relative densities, relative scores, and the log-Sobolev convention
steps.body:
Use a density relative to the target, rather than to Lebesgue measure: \( ho=r u\). When \( u(dx)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}dx\) and \( ho(dx)=p(x)dx\), this means \(r=Zpe^U\), so the relative score is \(s= abla\log r= abla\log p+ abla U\). The basic quantities are

\[ H_ u( ho)=\int r\log r\,d u, \qquad J_ u( ho)=\int\| abla\log r\|^2\,d ho. \]

The normalization is \(2\alpha H_ u( ho)\leq J_ u( ho)\). A factor of two in the LSI convention would change every stated rate, so this normalization is part of the comparison with the paper. The target is a probability measure, and the stated log-Sobolev hypothesis is tested on strictly positive, continuously differentiable relative densities defining probability measures. For the density \(r\), Fisher information is the nonnegative, possibly infinite integral of the squared relative score. An extension from that test class to arbitrary densities is not asserted here.

To compare conventions, for a positive smooth function \(g\) with \(\int g^2d u=1\), put \(r=g^2\). Then \(\int r\| abla\log r\|^2d u=4\int\| abla g\|^2d u\). This explains the familiar LSI convention \(\operatorname{Ent}_ u(g^2)\leq(2/\alpha)\int\| abla g\|^2d u\). This calculation identifies the constants in the two conventions. The assumed inequality is the relative-density formulation above, restricted to the stated positive smooth test class.

steps.title: Finiteness of relative entropy and Fisher information
steps.body:
Entropy here is the relative entropy of the probability laws. This divergence and the Fisher information take values in \([0,\infty]\). An ordinary real-valued comparison is used only after the finiteness of each quantity has been established.

When both extended quantities are finite, the log-Sobolev inequality gives \(2\alpha H\leq J\) over the reals. The density argument also proves finite relative entropy along each identified interpolation path. Its value at time zero is the entropy of the corresponding current ULA law, including the initial law. These identifications ensure that the real entropy used in the scalar recurrence is the finite relative entropy of the stated probability distribution.

sections.title: The Gaussian interpolation law and its second moments
sections.intro: The frozen-drift interpolation is \(Y_t=X-t\nabla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\), with independent standard Gaussian \(Z\). These elementary law and energy results precede the analytic density construction. The subsequent analysis proves density and entropy regularity for this same law.

steps.title: The interpolation transition and its values at the step boundaries
steps.body:
Define the interpolation law by applying \((x,z)\mapsto x-t\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}\,z\) to \(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)\). The product measure expresses the required independence. The ULA laws are obtained by iterating the time-step transition, starting from \(\mu\).

\[ \operatorname{Law}(Y_0)=\rho_k, \qquad \operatorname{Law}(Y_h)=\rho_{k+1}. \]

The zero-time identity needs no regularity of \(U\). Lipschitz continuity of \(\nabla U\) supplies measurability of the update and proves probability preservation; iteration proves that all \(\rho_k\) are probability laws. These statements identify the algorithm that the final entropy bound concerns. They do not provide a smooth density for the pushforward or differentiate its entropy. Although the law definition accepts a real time parameter, its frozen-drift Gaussian interpretation in this argument is for \(t\geq0\).

steps.title: Gaussian second moments and cancellation of the mixed term
steps.body:
The noise contribution is exactly dimension dependent: \(\mathbb E\|Z\|^2=n\). Expanding the squared norm in an orthonormal basis and using unit variance of each standard Gaussian coordinate gives this equality. The sum of coordinate variances has this value in every finite dimension, including zero.

More generally, if \(g\) is square integrable under a probability law \(\mu\), independence and the zero Gaussian mean give

\[ \mathbb E_{\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)} \|a\,g(X)+bZ\|^2 =a^2\mathbb E_\mu\|g(X)\|^2+b^2n. \]

The proof first establishes integrability of the squared terms and the inner-product cross term. The latter integral is \(\langle\mathbb Eg(X),\mathbb EZ\rangle=0\). Thus cancellation is an equality on the independent product law, rather than an estimate that hides a factor of two. This exact calculation is the source of the \(2tn\) noise term below.

steps.title: Displacement energy and the gradient discrepancy
steps.body:
The initial position cancels from the displacement: \(Y_t-X=-t\nabla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}\,Z\). Let \(G_k=\mathbb E_{\rho_k}\|\nabla U(X)\|^2\). Provided the gradient is square integrable, the affine Gaussian identity gives

\[ \mathbb E\|Y_t-X\|^2=t^2G_k+2tn. \]

No second moment of \(X\) itself is needed for this identity. The separate integrability proof concerns the displacement and the gradient. Applying the \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient bound pointwise, squaring, and integrating yields

\[ \mathbb E\|\nabla U(Y_t)-\nabla U(X)\|^2 \leq L^2(t^2G_k+2tn). \]

The displacement estimate proves square integrability of the joint gradient discrepancy as well as the displayed energy bound. Taking its conditional expectation given the interpolated state gives a measurable state-dependent error field; conditional Jensen preserves the same bound. The Gaussian weak equation and bounded-log entropy argument can instead use the joint discrepancy directly. This latter argument does not require a time-dependent choice of conditional-error representatives.

sections.title: Relative entropy and score calculus
sections.intro: The following density identities concern relative entropy, the relative score, and differentiation under explicit local domination assumptions. The Gaussian interpolation analysis subsequently verifies the density and entropy properties needed for its own entropy-production formula.

steps.title: Change of measure and the density formulas for entropy and Fisher information
steps.body:
For a measurable nonnegative \(r\), change of measure gives \(\int g\,d(r u)=\int rg\,d u\). The Radon–Nikodym derivative of the tilted measure with respect to \( u\) is the specified density, almost everywhere. Consequently its log-likelihood ratio is \(\log r\), almost everywhere for the tilted measure.

When \(r u\) and \( u\) are probability measures and \(r\log r\) is integrable, the relative entropy is finite and its real value is precisely

\[ H_ u(r u)=\int r\log r\,d u. \]

These measure-theoretic identifications justify using the familiar density formula in the subsequent calculus. The analogous Fisher formula is \(J_ u(r u)=\int r\| abla\log r\|^2d u\), with squared-score integrability retained. Positivity and smoothness will make the score well defined pointwise; the measure-change identities themselves need less regularity.

The density change of measure also shows that integrability of \(\log r\) under \(r u\) is exactly integrability of \(r\log r\) under \( u\). Consequently the asserted finite entropy includes absolute continuity and integrability of the log-likelihood ratio. Likewise, integrability of the squared relative score proves finite Fisher information. Each density formula is therefore an identity of finite integrals when it is used as a real-valued quantity.

steps.title: Differentiation of the entropy integral under a local integrable bound
steps.body:
At a positive density value, ordinary calculus gives \(\partial_t(r_t\log r_t)=\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\). Passing this derivative through an integral requires more than the pointwise chain rule. Assume local measurability, integrability at the time under consideration, and the existence of an integrable function \(B(x)\) dominating \(|\dot r_u(x)(\log r_u(x)+1)|\) on a common time neighborhood. Pointwise differentiability and positivity hold there for almost every spatial point.

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\int r_t\log r_t\,d\nu =\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\,d\nu. \]

Dominated differentiation then proves integrability of the differentiated integrand and the stated derivative formula. The sufficient local assumptions concern the density, its pointwise time derivative, and the common dominating function; the derivative of the entropy integral is their conclusion. The common neighborhood and integrable bound are substantive analytic requirements for an application, particularly at the initial interpolation time.

steps.title: The entropy test and Fisher dissipation
steps.body:
Positivity gives the pointwise identities

\[ \nabla\log r=\frac{\nabla r}{r},\qquad \nabla(\log r+1)=\nabla\log r,\qquad \langle\nabla r,\nabla(\log r+1)\rangle =r\|\nabla\log r\|^2. \]

The first identity is the gradient chain rule. The second explains why the normalization term \(+1\), introduced by differentiating \(r\log r\), contributes no spatial derivative. The third is the algebraic source of Fisher dissipation. These are pointwise differential identities and require no integration by parts or stochastic evolution equation.

For an exact Langevin density with an admissible unforced weak equation, this calculation would give \(H'=-J\). The conditional continuous-time theorem combines that identity with LSI to obtain \(H(t)\leq e^{-2\alpha t}H(0)\). The ULA interpolation has an additional frozen-drift error, so its argument continues with a forced equation.

The unforced weak-identity theorem makes this reference calculation precise: take the same admissible entropy test with the error field absent, and the production integral is exactly minus the weighted squared-score integral. The scalar differential inequality then gives the rate \(2\alpha\). To interpret it as an entropy bound, the scalar quantities must be identified with finite relative entropy and Fisher information of a density path satisfying the stated weak equation. These density and dissipation hypotheses are explicit in this intermediate calculation. This separation is also useful for ULA: the same dissipation calculation survives, and only the explicitly displayed error contribution changes.

sections.title: The weak equation and the drift-error contribution
sections.intro: The forced relative-density weak equation has a gradient-discrepancy term. Young’s inequality bounds its pairing with the relative score by one quarter of the Fisher information plus the squared error energy. These auxiliary calculations assume the displayed weak equation. The subsequent Gaussian argument proves that equation for bounded tests and justifies the logarithmic limit.

steps.title: The forced weak equation and the logarithmic test
steps.body:
Suppose the relative density satisfies, for each admissible continuously differentiable test \(\psi\),

\[ \int\dot r_t\psi\,d\nu =-\int\langle\nabla r_t,\nabla\psi\rangle\,d\nu +\int r_t\langle e_t,\nabla\psi\rangle\,d\nu. \]

For frozen drift, the intended error is \(e_t(y)=\nabla U(y)-\mathbb E[\nabla U(X)\mid Y_t=y]\). This formula explains the sign convention. Conditional expectation gives such a field. The subsequent Gaussian argument proves its weak equation directly from the transition density and may retain the joint discrepancy instead. At this stage the weak identity is assumed with the stated field \(e_t\).

Choose \(\psi=\log r_t+1\). The score identities then give

\[ H'(t)=-J(t)+\int r_t\langle e_t,s_t\rangle\,d\nu. \]

The hypothesis permits the test whenever its three integrands are integrable. Since \(\log r_t+1\) generally has noncompact support, a generator identity proved only for compactly supported tests does not automatically establish this hypothesis. The passage to this entropy test needs its own analytic justification.

steps.title: Young’s inequality with three quarters of Fisher dissipation retained
steps.body:
The pointwise Young inequality used here is

\[ \langle e,s\rangle\leq\frac14\|s\|^2+\|e\|^2. \]

It follows from Cauchy–Schwarz and \((\|e\|-\|s\|/2)^2\geq0\). Multiplication by \(r\geq0\) and integration yield

\[ H'(t)\leq-\frac34J(t)+\mathcal E(t), \qquad \mathcal E(t)=\int r_t\|e_t\|^2\,d\nu. \]

The coefficient \(3/4\) is deliberate: the drift-score interaction is at most one quarter of the Fisher information plus the error energy, leaving enough dissipation for the scalar contraction estimate. The same calculation bounds the absolute value of the inner product. With measurability and finite score and error energies, that version establishes integrability of the cross term; cross-term integrability is proved before the identity is integrated.

steps.title: The entropy derivative from regular density data and the weak equation
steps.body:
Combine the dominated time derivative, the KL density formula, the entropy test, and Young's inequality. The conclusion concerns relative entropy, with a right derivative on the interpolation interval, and the bound \(-3J/4+\mathcal E\). Its inputs include positive spatially \(C^1\) densities, normalization, local entropy regularity, integrability of the squared score, the error energy, and the admissible forced weak equation.

The accompanying continuity theorem derives continuity of relative entropy on the closed interval from the same density data. Thus these density hypotheses imply both entropy continuity and the required derivative formula. It leaves the quantitative estimate on \(\mathcal E(t)\) to be supplied. In the intended Gaussian application that estimate is

\[ \mathcal E(t)\leq t^2L^2G_k+2tnL^2. \]

The joint Gaussian estimate established earlier has exactly the required right-hand side. Conditional expectation constructs the error field with the same energy bound and preserves its integrable flux tests. The Gaussian analysis below proves the weak equation from the kernel, and bounded logarithmic tests give the time chain rule and its untruncated limit.

There are two equivalent formulations. One concerns the ordinary integral \(\int r_t\log r_t\,d\nu\). The other first identifies that integral with relative entropy, using normalization and finite entropy, then supplies the right derivative needed on \([0,h]\). The density-law identification is needed to pass from differentiation of an integral to a statement about the relative entropy of the ULA law.

sections.title: The scalar one-step entropy estimate
sections.intro: Fix one interpolation interval and abbreviate its entropy by \(H(t)\), its real Fisher information by \(I(t)\), and its initial squared-gradient moment by \(G_0\). At this stage the argument is scalar. The theorem below derives the one-step recurrence from the displayed differential and moment inequalities.

steps.title: The entropy-production, log-Sobolev, and gradient-moment inequalities
steps.body:
The required estimates on \(0\leq t \[ 2\alpha H(t)\leq I(t),\qquad H'(t)\leq-\frac34I(t)+t^2L^2G_0+2tnL^2, \] \[ G_0\leq\frac{4L^2}{\alpha}H(0)+2nL. \]

Also assume \(H(0)\geq0\), entropy continuity on \([0,h]\), the indicated right derivatives, \(n\geq0\), and the numerical regime \(0<\alpha\leq L\), \(0

Substituting LSI into production leaves \(-3\alpha H(t)/2\), plus positive forcing. Because that forcing includes the initial entropy through \(G_0\), it is not enough simply to invoke exponential decay at rate \(3\alpha/2\). The next calculation bounds and then absorbs this initial-entropy contribution.

steps.title: A time-independent upper bound for the forcing
steps.body:
The step restriction and \(\alpha\leq L\) imply \(hL\leq1/4\) and \(\alpha h\leq1/4\). Define

\[ A=\frac{4L^2}{\alpha}H(0)+2nL. \]

Then \(G_0\leq A\) and \(A\geq0\). Squaring \(hL^2\leq\alpha/4\) gives

\[ h^2L^2\frac{4L^2}{\alpha}\leq\frac\alpha4. \]

The other part uses \(hL\leq1/4\): \(h^2L^2(2nL)\leq hnL^2/2\). Therefore

\[ h^2L^2A\leq\frac\alpha4H(0)+\frac12hnL^2. \]

For \(0\leq t \[ b=\frac\alpha4H(0)+\frac52hnL^2, \qquad H'(t)\leq-\frac32\alpha H(t)+b. \]

Thus the original time-dependent forcing is bounded by the constant displayed above. Every multiplication uses the nonnegative initial entropy, dimension, and step length. Substitution in the entropy-production inequality gives the asserted constant-forcing differential inequality.

steps.title: Integration of the affine differential inequality
steps.body:
For \(a>0\), continuity and right derivatives satisfying \(H'\leq-aH+b\) imply the exact affine comparison

\[ H(t)\leq e^{-at}H(0)+\frac ba(1-e^{-at}). \]

The proof uses a right-derivative Grönwall comparison; the scalar lemma needs no sign assumption on \(H\) or \(b\). Apply it with \(a=3\alpha/2\). In this application \(b\geq0\), and the elementary tangent bound for the exponential gives \((1-e^{-ah})/a\leq h\). Consequently

\[ H(h)\leq \left(e^{-3\alpha h/2}+\frac{\alpha h}{4}\right)H(0) +\frac52h^2nL^2. \]

This expression contains the additional coefficient of the initial entropy. The exponential comparison in the next step combines it with the decay factor, so the bound has no separate additive multiple of \(H(0)\) at each step.

steps.title: The exponential comparison and the one-step coefficient
steps.body:
Put \(x=\alpha h\in[0,1/4]\). The exponential comparison is

\[ e^{-3x/2}+\frac x4\leq e^{-x}. \]

Indeed, \(e^{x/2}\geq1+x/2\), so \(e^{-x}-e^{-3x/2}\geq e^{-3x/2}x/2\). On this interval the tangent bound gives \(e^{-3x/2}\geq1/2\), making the gap at least \(x/4\). Multiplication by nonnegative \(H(0)\) absorbs the extra term from the uniform forcing.

The resulting noise coefficient \(5/2\) can be enlarged to the paper's coefficient \(6\). Thus the scalar conclusion is

\[ H(h)\leq e^{-\alpha h}H(0)+6h^2nL^2. \]

The intermediate constant is smaller than the stated final constant. The paper uses a different integrating-factor and exponential estimate. The present calculation has the same hypotheses, contraction factor, and coefficient \(6\); it does not claim to reproduce every intermediate scalar line of the appendix.

sections.title: Iteration of the entropy estimate
sections.intro: After identifying the two endpoint densities with the ULA laws, the previous result becomes \(H_{k+1}\leq qH_k+c\), with \(q=e^{-\alpha h}\in(0,1)\) and \(c=6h^2nL^2\). The last step is an exact scalar recurrence calculation followed by a small-step denominator bound.

steps.title: The finite geometric sum for the affine entropy recurrence
steps.body:
Iterating the affine recurrence gives

\[ H_k\leq q^kH_0+c\frac{1-q^k}{1-q} =e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+ 6h^2nL^2\frac{1-e^{-\alpha hk}}{1-e^{-\alpha h}}. \]

This follows by induction: multiply the preceding bound by the nonnegative coefficient and add the next forcing term. The resulting finite geometric sum has the displayed value. No sign assumption on \(H_0\) is needed for the exact recurrence statement, although finite relative entropy is nonnegative. The expression exhibits both accumulation of discretization error and its bounded geometric saturation.

The persistent term in the published bound is obtained by replacing \(1-q^k\) by at most one and controlling \(1-q\) from below. The recurrence by itself does not identify \(H_k\) with the entropy of a particular algorithm. The preceding interpolation-law identities provide that identification for ULA.

steps.title: The denominator bound and the final coefficient
steps.body:
For \(0\leq x\leq1/4\), the exponential estimate is

\[ 1-e^{-x}\geq\frac34x. \]

The exponential tangent inequality gives \(e^{-x}\leq1/(1+x)\), hence \(1-e^{-x}\geq x/(1+x)\geq3x/4\) on this interval. Substitute \(x=\alpha h\) and use positivity of the denominator:

\[ \frac{6h^2nL^2}{1-e^{-\alpha h}} \leq\frac{6h^2nL^2}{(3/4)\alpha h} =\frac{8hnL^2}{\alpha}. \]

This explains the final coefficient \(8\). The step restriction together with \(\alpha\leq L\) provides \(\alpha h\leq1/4\); the numerical compatibility is therefore used by the current proof and is required for this denominator estimate.

sections.title: Entropy estimates under explicit density hypotheses
sections.intro: These intermediate results apply to density paths with explicitly stated regularity, law, weak-equation, and moment hypotheses. They derive an entropy estimate from those data. The final Gaussian ULA argument below instead constructs its positive-time density and proves the almost-everywhere entropy derivative, so those analytic data are not separate hypotheses of the final theorem.

steps.title: The one-step and iterated bounds under explicit interpolation hypotheses
steps.body:
Supply a family \(r_{k,t}\) with \(r_{k,t}\nu=\operatorname{Law}(Y_t)\) for every \(k\) and \(t\in[0,h]\). Positivity and spatial \(C^1\) regularity make each density admissible for the LSI test class. Probability follows from the Gaussian law identification. Finite KL and Fisher information make the real LSI inequality legitimate. Continuity, right derivatives, the production bound, and the per-step gradient-moment bound supply the scalar theorem's remaining inputs.

The zero-time and endpoint law identities turn \(H(0)\) and \(H(h)\) into \(H_k\) and \(H_{k+1}\). The one-step comparison then gives the coefficient-\(6\) estimate. Iteration of the recurrence identifies the entropy at step zero as \(H_\nu(\mu)\). The discrete entropy recurrence is a conclusion of these path hypotheses.

The potential differentiability and squared-gradient integrability premises remain explicit in this interface, alongside the quantified gradient-moment estimate. Their presence should not be read as a proof of that estimate.

steps.title: A sufficient set of density-regularity hypotheses
steps.body:
Suppose the interpolation has density derivatives \(\dot r_{k,t}\), error fields \(e_{k,t}\), and local entropy regularity data. Assume also spatial positivity and smoothness, squared-score integrability, integrable drift energy, measurability of the drift-score term, and the forced weak equation for all admissible continuously differentiable tests.

These assumptions imply finite relative entropy, finite Fisher information, entropy continuity, the right derivative of relative entropy, and \(H'\leq-3J/4+\mathcal E\). The separately supplied drift-energy bound then gives the required production estimate. Applying the preceding conditional entropy estimate shows that neither entropy derivatives, the production inequality, nor the discrete recurrence need be assumed at this level.

This sufficient set of hypotheses retains the density-law identity, local regularity data, admissible weak equation, drift-energy and gradient-moment estimates, and compatibility. The completed Gaussian route below proves the corresponding probability-law conclusions using bounded log tests and almost-everywhere entropy calculus, then gives the final ULA theorem from the original assumptions.

steps.title: Use of the same analytic assumptions for a transformed interpolation
steps.body:
Suppose one has the same density functions, local domination, score integrability, admissible weak equation, drift-energy estimate, and gradient-moment estimate used above. These assumptions concern the density and its analytic properties. Entropy derivatives, the one-step estimate, and convergence are their consequences. For a new interpolation, the displayed analytic conditions must therefore be proved or explicitly assumed.

Equality with the Gaussian law identifies the densities as normalized probability densities. The local regularity at time zero gives finite entropy of the current algorithm law. Together with the log-Sobolev, smoothness, and numerical hypotheses, the entropy test gives the coefficient-\(6\) recurrence, and iteration gives the coefficient-\(8\) bound.

This interface is useful for a change of coordinates or a particle construction: one can specify the lifted potential, its Gaussian step, and the same analytic conditions, then reuse the proved entropy calculation. The IPLA entropy extension explains the particle scaling and its additional lifted-target LSI hypothesis.

sections.title: The positive Gaussian mixture and its density relative to Gibbs
sections.intro:
Let \(\mu\) be the initial probability, \(t>0\), and \(c_t(x)=x-t abla U(x)\). The update \(c_t(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\), with \(Z\) an independent standard Gaussian vector, has density \(q_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\), where \(K_t(x,y)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\exp(-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2/(4t))\). This follows by conditioning on \(X\) and applying Tonelli. No initial Lebesgue density is needed.

Each Gaussian component is positive and bounded by \((4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). The mixture is consequently positive and finite at every observation. Dominated convergence gives spatial continuity, and parameter integration gives measurability. If the Gibbs probability has density \(J(y)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}\), the positive continuous function \(r_t=q_t/J=Ze^Uq_t\) satisfies \(r_t u=q_tdy\) and \(\int r_td u=1\). Its differentiability, entropy, and Fisher information require the subsequent estimates.

steps.title: The nonnegative Gaussian mixture integral
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), put \(c_t(x)=x-t\nabla U(x)\) and \(C_t=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). Define

\[K_t(x,y)=C_t\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-c_t(x)\|^2}{4t}\right),\qquad q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x).\]

For fixed \(x\), this is the Gaussian density with mean \(c_t(x)\) and covariance \(2tI_d\). The mixture is initially defined by a nonnegative integral, which may take the value infinity. Tonelli is therefore available before a pointwise finiteness assertion has been proved.

The subsequent peak bound will show that this same integral is finite at every \(y\), even for an initial law with no density or moments. The positive-time assumption is used in the Gaussian normalization and denominator.

steps.title: Apply measurable parameter integration to the mixture
steps.body:
A Lipschitz gradient is continuous and measurable, so \(c_t\) is measurable in the starting point. The map \((x,y)\mapsto y-c_t(x)\) is jointly measurable. Squared norm, multiplication by the fixed scalar, and exponential preserve measurability, so \(K_t\) is a jointly measurable nonnegative kernel.

Integration in \(x\) against \(\mu\) yields a measurable function of \(y\). The mixing measure is finite and hence sigma-finite, as required for measurable parameter integration. This measurability assertion concerns the defining formula and does not use a positive-time finiteness estimate.

steps.title: The update law has the Gaussian mixture density
steps.body:
Let \(X\sim\mu\), let \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\) be independent, and write \(Y_t=c_t(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\). For a measurable set \(A\), independence and the pushforward formula give

\[\mathbb P(Y_t\in A)=\int\mathbb P\bigl(c_t(x)+\sqrt{2t}Z\in A\bigr)d\mu(x).\]

The inner probability is \(\int_AK_t(x,y)dy\), by the fixed-state affine Gaussian density. Joint measurability permits Tonelli under \(\mu\) and Lebesgue measure restricted to \(A\). Consequently

\[\mathbb P(Y_t\in A)=\int_A\left(\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\right)dy=\int_Aq_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)dy.\]

Thus the mixture is the density of the update law. Equivalently, the same computation applies to every nonnegative measurable test function. It does not assume that \(\mu\) itself has a density.

steps.title: Use positivity of every Gaussian component
steps.body:
At positive time the normalizer \(C_t\) is strictly positive, and the exponential is strictly positive at every finite argument. Hence \(K_t(x,y)>0\) for every pair \(x,y\).

Fix \(y\). The nonnegative measurable function \(x\mapsto K_t(x,y)\) is positive on the whole state space, which has \(\mu\)-mass one. A nonnegative integral can vanish only when its integrand is zero almost everywhere. Therefore \(q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)>0\). This proves positivity at every observation, before any assertion about its finiteness.

steps.title: Bound every mixture value by the common Gaussian peak
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), the Gaussian exponent is nonpositive, hence

\[0\le K_t(x,y)\le C_t,\qquad q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\le C_t.\]

The proof establishes the exponential bound with the fact that an exponential with nonpositive exponent is at most one: the numerator \(-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2\) is nonpositive and the denominator \(4t\) is positive. Multiplication by the nonnegative normalizer preserves the inequality, and the same inequality holds for nonnegative extended values.

Monotonicity of the nonnegative integral integrates this pointwise bound. The integral of the constant \(C_t\) equals \(C_t\mu(E)=C_t\) because \(\mu\) is a probability measure. This theorem requires no regularity of the gradient: its bound concerns the nonnegative integrand at every point, and the upper nonnegative integral remains monotone even before measurability is established.

The exponential factor is at most one, independently of the Gaussian center. Hence averaging over any starting probability retains the same peak bound, without requiring an initial moment.

steps.title: Pointwise finiteness of the mixture
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\) and let \(C_t=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}<\infty\). Every Gaussian component satisfies \(0\le K_t(x,y)\le C_t\), independently of its center. Because \(\mu\) is a probability, integration in the starting point gives

\[0\le\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\le\int C_t d\mu=C_t<\infty.\]

Thus the initially nonnegative-integral definition of the mixture is finite at every observation \(y\). It has an ordinary real value pointwise, with the same peak bound, even if \(\mu\) has no density or position moments. The positive-time condition is essential: at zero the Gaussian peak need not have a finite limiting bound.

steps.title: The finite real-valued mixture density
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), the preceding peak bound makes the mixture finite at every observation. We therefore use its ordinary real-valued representative

\[p_t(y)=\int (4\pi t)^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-x+t\nabla U(x)\|^2}{4t}\right)d\mu(x).\]

This nonnegative integral is at most \((4\pi t)^{-d/2}\) and is strictly positive because every Gaussian component is positive and \(\mu\) is a probability. Its ordinary value and nonnegative extended value agree everywhere. The positive-time law identity, regularity statements, and logarithmic derivatives below all use this same finite representative.

steps.title: The update law has the finite density
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), write \(q_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\), which is finite everywhere by the preceding peak bound. For every measurable set \(A\), the proposal law satisfies

\[\begin{aligned} \rho_t(A)&=\int\left(\int_AK_t(x,y)dy\right)d\mu(x)\\ &=\int_A\left(\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\right)dy =\int_Aq_t(y)dy. \end{aligned}\]

The first identity conditions on the initial point and uses the affine Gaussian proposal density. The second is Tonelli for the nonnegative kernel. Its finite pointwise mixture is precisely the ordinary density defined above, so no change of law accompanies passage to real-valued density notation. This identification remains valid for singular initial laws.

steps.title: Deduce absolute continuity for every positive time
steps.body:
The law identity \(\rho_t=q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}dy\) immediately implies \(\rho_t\ll dy\): every Lebesgue-null set has zero integral against the density and thus zero proposal probability.

The interpolation law has density \(q_t\) with respect to Lebesgue measure. Hence a Lebesgue-null set has zero interpolation probability, proving absolute continuity at positive time. This holds even for singular initial laws. Finite KL with respect to Gibbs and entropy behavior at zero require the separate score and endpoint arguments.

The proposed law has a Lebesgue density, so every Lebesgue-null set has proposed mass zero. This absolute continuity holds for arbitrary initial laws once the elapsed Gaussian time is positive.

steps.title: The ordinary integral formula for the mixture
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\) and an observation \(y\). The real Gaussian kernel is measurable in \(x\), nonnegative, and bounded by \(C_t\). Since \(\mu\) is a probability, this constant is integrable, so the kernel has an ordinary finite integral.

For a nonnegative integrable function, its ordinary integral equals its nonnegative integral viewed as a real value. The finite mixture therefore satisfies

\[q_t(y)=\int C_t\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-c_t(x)\|^2}{4t}\right)d\mu(x).\]

The equality identifies two forms of the same integral. It does not change the probability law or choose a different density.

steps.title: Pass spatial continuity through the probability mixture
steps.body:
At a fixed positive time, \(q_t:E\to\mathbb R\) is continuous. For every fixed initial state \(x\), the Gaussian kernel \(y\mapsto K_t(x,y)\) is continuous, and its absolute value is bounded by the same constant \(C_t\), independent of \(x\) and \(y\).

The proof first replaces the explicit Gaussian-mixture Lebesgue density by the ordinary integral formula from the previous theorem. It applies continuity under an integral with the common integrable majorant \(x\mapsto C_t\). Measurability in \(x\) follows from gradient continuity. The nonpositive Gaussian exponent proves \(\|K_t(x,y)\|=K_t(x,y)\le C_t\); probability normalization makes this majorant integrable. Pointwise continuity in \(y\) is then assembled from subtraction, norm, square and exponential.

Dominated convergence therefore passes the pointwise kernel continuity through the mixture integral. The conclusion is spatial continuity; spatial and time differentiation require separate domination estimates.

At a fixed positive time the component kernel is continuous in the observation and bounded by one common peak. Dominated convergence passes that continuity through the mixture integral.

steps.title: Derive finite partition from target normalization
steps.body:
Write the normalized Gibbs measure as \( u=Z^{-1}(e^{-U}dy)\), where initially \(Z=\int e^{-U}dy\) is a nonnegative extended integral. Assume this normalized measure is a probability. If \(Z=\infty\), its reciprocal is zero, so \( u\) would be the zero measure, contradicting \( u(E)=1\). Thus \(Z<\infty\).

The separate positivity argument for the partition gives \(Z>0\) under the displayed assumptions. Together these facts make \(Z\) an ordinary positive finite denominator. This deduction uses target normalization and the partition's positivity, without a strong-convexity assumption. In particular it applies when probability normalization is part of the log-Sobolev hypothesis.

steps.title: Write the explicit density relative to Gibbs
steps.body:
The normalized Gibbs target has Lebesgue density \(Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}\). Therefore the relative density corresponding to the mixture \(q_t(y)dy\) is

\[r_t(y)=Z e^{U(y)}q_t(y).\]

The relative density is the ordinary product \(r_t(y)=Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y)\). The positive finite partition and mixture peak bounds make all factors finite at positive time. Multiplication by the Gibbs density cancels \(Ze^{U(y)}\), producing the Lebesgue density \(q_t\).

The definition makes the coordinate conversion explicit: the ratio to the target is obtained by multiplying the Lebesgue density by the reciprocal target density. Entropy differentiation, convergence, and weak differential equations are separate conclusions requiring their own hypotheses.

The Gibbs Lebesgue density is \(J(y)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}\), so the relative density is \(r_t(y)=Z e^{U(y)}p_t(y)\). Multiplying by \(J\) recovers \(p_t\) pointwise.

steps.title: Multiply measurable factors to obtain relative-density measurability
steps.body: Write the relative density as \(r_t(y)=Ze^{U(y)}p_t(y)\). The mixture \(p_t\) is measurable by parameter integration; differentiability of \(U\) gives measurability of \(e^U\); and the partition \(Z\) is a fixed finite scalar. Products of these measurable factors are measurable. Thus the explicit relative density is measurable, as required to define its weighted target measure. This statement is a measurability conclusion; spatial differentiation and finite entropy are established separately.

steps.title: Obtain relative-density continuity at positive time
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), the mixture \(q_t\) is spatially continuous by the Gaussian peak domination argument. Differentiability of the potential implies continuity of \(U\), so \(y\mapsto e^{U(y)}\) is continuous. The partition \(Z\) is a fixed finite scalar.

Multiplying these continuous factors proves continuity of \(r_t(y)=Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y)\). Equivalently, the Gibbs density \(J\) is continuous and everywhere positive, so \(r_t=q_t/J\) has no singular denominator. This proves continuity only; the differentiability required for the log-Sobolev application follows from the subsequent Gaussian derivative estimates.

steps.title: Strict positivity of the relative density
steps.body:
Assume the Gibbs target is a probability and \(t>0\). The partition positivity result and target normalization give \(0<Z<\infty\). The Gaussian peak and positivity results give \(0<q_t(y)<\infty\) at every observation. The ordinary exponential \(e^{U(y)}\) is also finite and strictly positive.

Every factor in \(r_t(y)=Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y)\) is therefore a positive finite real number, proving \(r_t(y)>0\). Both positivity and finiteness are needed: neither an infinite mixture value nor a zero partition could be used as an ordinary positive relative density.

steps.title: The relative density represents the update law
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\) and assume the Gibbs partition satisfies \(0<Z<\infty\), as proved under the target normalization hypotheses. Let

\[J(y)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)},\qquad r_t(y)=Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y).\]

The mixture \(q_t\) is finite and measurable, and the Gibbs density is strictly positive. Pointwise multiplication therefore gives the ordinary identity

\[r_t(y)J(y)=\bigl(Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y)\bigr)\bigl(Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}\bigr)=q_t(y).\]

Integrating over any measurable set identifies the measures:

\[r_t\nu=q_tdy=\rho_t.\]

The last equality is the Gaussian-mixture law identity already proved. Hence this relative density represents the specified interpolation law. Positivity, spatial regularity, time differentiation, and finite entropy remain separate properties established in the subsequent analysis.

steps.title: Normalization of the relative density
steps.body:
The measure induced by the constructed relative density is a probability measure:

\[\int r_t\,d u=1\qquad(t>0).\]

Integrating the identity \(r_t u= ho_t\) over the entire state space gives \(\int r_t\,d u=1\), because the Gaussian update is a probability law. Thus the explicitly constructed density is normalized; no separate assumption about its mass is required.

Positivity, continuity, and normalization all concern this same density. Normalization alone does not imply finite entropy or Fisher information; these properties will follow from the positive-time moment and derivative bounds.

Integrating the law identity on the whole space gives \(\int r_t\,d u=1\). Normalization is therefore inherited from the Gaussian transition rather than proved by a separate algebraic manipulation of a possibly infinite density.

sections.title: Conditional expectation of the Gaussian drift discrepancy
sections.intro: Let \(Y\) be an observed random variable and let \(D\) be a square-integrable random vector. Under the stated measurability assumptions, the conditional expectation given \(\sigma(Y)\) has a measurable representation \(e(Y)\). Conditional Jensen gives \(\int\|e\|^2d(Y_\#P)\le\mathbb E\|D\|^2\). Applied to \(D_t=\nabla U(Y_t)-\nabla U(X)\), this produces the state-dependent discrepancy in the relative-density weak equation and preserves the Gaussian energy bound.

steps.title: A measurable representation of a conditional mean
steps.body:
Let \(P\) be a probability measure on the underlying sample space, let \(Y:\Omega\to S\) be measurable, and let \(D\) take values in a real Banach space with its Borel sigma algebra.

Assume \(D\in L^2(P)\) and \(Y\) is measurable. The conditional expectation \(\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\) is strongly measurable with respect to \(\sigma(Y)\). Doob–Dynkin factorization, under the stated assumptions on the spaces, gives a strongly measurable field \(e\) such that \(e(Y)=\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\) almost surely. Conditional Jensen and integration give

\[\int\|e(y)\|^2d(Y_\#P)(y)=\mathbb E\|\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\|^2\le\mathbb E\|D\|^2.\]

The conditional expectation is square-integrable, so the integral on the left is finite. The field is determined only up to a null set under the law of \(Y\), which does not affect these integrals.

steps.title: The conditional mean on measurable sets
steps.body:
Suppose \(D\) is integrable and \(e(Y)=\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\) almost surely. For every measurable observation set \(A\), the pushforward integral formula and the defining property of conditional expectation give

\[\int_A e(y)d(Y_\#P)(y)=\int_{Y^{-1}(A)}e(Y)\,dP=\int_{Y^{-1}(A)}D\,dP.\]

The inverse image \(Y^{-1}(A)\) belongs to \(\sigma(Y)\), so the last equality is a valid conditional-expectation identity. All terms are vector-valued integrals under the stated integrability assumptions.

steps.title: Pairing the conditional mean with an observed test
steps.body:
Let \(\varphi\) be strongly measurable, and assume \(\langle D,\varphi(Y)\rangle\) is integrable. The function \(\varphi(Y)\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(Y)\). The conditional expectation rule for a continuous bilinear pairing therefore gives

\[\mathbb E[\langle D,\varphi(Y)\rangle\mid\sigma(Y)]=\langle\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)],\varphi(Y)\rangle.\]

Integrate this equality, replace the conditional mean by \(e(Y)\), and change variables by the law of \(Y\). The result is

\[\int\langle e(y),\varphi(y)\rangle d(Y_\#P)(y)=\mathbb E\langle D,\varphi(Y)\rangle.\]

The integrability hypothesis is required for this test; it is not inferred for arbitrary unbounded functions.

steps.title: The gradient discrepancy before conditioning
steps.body:
On the product space of the initial state and independent Gaussian variable, put \(Y_t(x,z)=x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\) and define

\[D_t(x,z)= abla U\!\left(x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z ight)- abla U(x).\]

Thus \(D_t= abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\). The order of subtraction fixes its sign in the weak equation: the conditional field is \(e_t(y)= abla U(y)-\mathbb E[ abla U(X)\mid Y_t=y]\). The definition alone asserts no integrability or energy bound.

steps.title: The sigma-algebra of the interpolated state
steps.body: The observation at elapsed time \(t\) is \(Y_t\), and its sigma-algebra is \(\sigma(Y_t)=\{Y_t^{-1}(A):A\text{ measurable}\}\), interpreted as the generated sigma-algebra. A random variable measurable for this sigma-algebra depends only on the value of \(Y_t\). Conditioning the gradient discrepancy on \(\sigma(Y_t)\) therefore yields a field on the state space. If the gradient is Lipschitz, the observation map is measurable and this sigma-algebra is contained in the ambient one.

steps.title: The conditional discrepancy and its second moment
steps.body:
Assume \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(G_0=\int\|\nabla U\|^2d\mu<\infty\). The Gaussian displacement estimate proves that \(D_t\) is square-integrable and \(\mathbb E\|D_t\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2tn)\), where \(n=\dim E\). Apply the measurable conditional-mean result to obtain a strongly measurable field \(e_t\) satisfying

\[e_t(Y_t)=\mathbb E[D_t\mid\sigma(Y_t)],\qquad \int\|e_t(y)\|^2d\rho_t(y)\le t^2L^2G_0+2tnL^2,\]\[\rho_t=(Y_t)_\#(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)).\]

The equality identifies the field for the same Gaussian interpolation used in the algorithm. Its square-integrability and energy bound follow from conditional Jensen and the preceding joint Gaussian estimate.

steps.title: The discrepancy energy relative to the Gibbs measure
steps.body:
Suppose a measurable nonnegative density identifies the interpolation law as \( ho_t=r_t u\). The conditional-mean construction gives a square-integrable field under \( ho_t\). Changing measure proves integrability of the weighted square under \( u\), and

\[\int r_t(y)\|e_t(y)\|^2d u(y)=\int\|e_t(y)\|^2d ho_t(y)\le t^2L^2G_0+2tnL^2.\]

The conditional-mean identity is unchanged. This is the form of the energy estimate that appears in entropy production.

sections.title: The gradient second moment from a transport coupling
sections.intro: Let \((X,Y)\) couple \(\mu\) and \( u\), with finite squared distance, and suppose the gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz. The inequality \(\| abla U(X)\|\le L\|X-Y\|+\| abla U(Y)\|\) gives a second-moment bound under \(\mu\) when that moment is finite under \( u\). For a normalized Gibbs target, the latter is at most \(nL\). An explicitly assumed entropy bound on the coupling cost then gives the stated entropy-dependent gradient estimate. The final ULA entropy theorem instead obtains its gradient moment directly from exponential integrability of the Gibbs score.

steps.title: Integrability and the coupling estimate
steps.body:
Let \(c\) have marginals \(\mu, u\), and assume \(\int\|x-y\|^2dc<\infty\) and \(\int\| abla U\|^2d u<\infty\). Lipschitzness and \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) give the pointwise inequality

\[\| abla U(x)\|^2\le2L^2\|x-y\|^2+2\| abla U(y)\|^2.\]

The right-hand side is integrable under \(c\). Measurability and domination imply integrability of the first-coordinate gradient square, hence of \(\| abla U\|^2\) under \(\mu\). Integration and the marginal identities give

\[\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu\le2L^2\int\|x-y\|^2dc(x,y)+2\int\| abla U\|^2d u.\]

steps.title: The estimate for a Gibbs target
steps.body:
Let \( u=Z^{-1}e^{-U}dx\) be a Gibbs probability measure, with differentiable \(U\) and \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Probability normalization supplies a finite positive partition function. The Gibbs score estimate proves square-integrability and \(\int\| abla U\|^2d u\le nL\), without strong convexity. Substituting these facts in the coupling estimate gives

\[\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu\le2L^2\int\|x-y\|^2dc+2nL.\]

The same argument proves gradient square-integrability under \(\mu\); it is not assumed before this conclusion.

steps.title: Substitution of an entropy bound on the coupling cost
steps.body:
Suppose the given finite-cost coupling also satisfies

\[\int\|x-y\|^2dc(x,y)\le rac2\alpha\operatorname{KL}(\mu\mid u),\qquad \alpha>0,\quad \operatorname{KL}(\mu\mid u)<\infty.\]

Multiply this inequality by \(2L^2\ge0\) and substitute it in the preceding gradient estimate. Since \(2L^2(2/\alpha)=4L^2/\alpha\),

\[\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu\le rac{4L^2}{\alpha}\operatorname{KL}(\mu\mid u)+2nL.\]

The cost-to-entropy estimate is an explicit hypothesis for the supplied coupling. This result does not prove a transport inequality from LSI.

sections.title: Entropy comparison with positive-time derivatives
sections.intro: A continuous function on \([0,T]\) can satisfy an affine comparison using derivative bounds only on \((0,T)\). This applies to Gaussian entropy calculations where derivatives are first proved at positive times. The second result identifies the relative-entropy derivative with the differentiated density integral at an interior time, under the stated local domination assumptions. Control near zero is required separately when passing to the initial law.

steps.title: An affine comparison without endpoint derivatives
steps.body:
Let \(a>0\), assume \(H\) is continuous on \([0,T]\), and suppose \(H'(t)\le-aH(t)+b\) on \((0,T)\). Set \(F(t)=e^{at}(H(t)-b/a)\). Then

\[F'(t)=e^{at}\bigl(a(H(t)-b/a)+H'(t)\bigr)\le0.\]

The mean-value theorem implies that \(F\) is nonincreasing on the closed interval, using continuity at its endpoints and differentiability in its interior. Thus \(F(t)\le F(0)\). Multiplication by \(e^{-at}>0\) and rearrangement give

\[H(t)\le e^{-at}H(0)+\frac ba(1-e^{-at}).\]

The cancellation \(a(b/a)=b\) uses \(a\ne0\). No derivative is required at zero or at \(T\).

steps.title: The entropy derivative at an interior time
steps.body:
Fix \(0\[ rac d{dt}\operatorname{KL}(r_t u\mid u)=\int\dot r_t(x)(\log r_t(x)+1)\,d u(x).\]

The assumptions concern interior times only. Continuity or a one-sided bound at zero must still be proved before applying an estimate that involves the initial entropy.

sections.title: The upper bound on the log-Sobolev constant
sections.intro:
Let \( u(dx)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}dx\) on a nontrivial finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. Suppose \(U\) is differentiable, \( abla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and the target satisfies the stated positive \(C^1\)-density log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\alpha\). Then \(\alpha\le L\). No position moment, Hessian, or strong convexity is assumed.

For bounded \(C^1\) tests with \(\| abla f\|\le D\), apply the inequality to normalized exponential tilts. The small-tilt limit gives \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}_ u(f)\le D^2\). For a unit vector \(v\), Gibbs integration by parts applied to \(\sin(t\langle v,x angle)\), together with the directional score second-moment bound \(L\), gives \(\alpha(\int\cos(t\langle v,x angle)d u)^2\le L\). Bounded convergence as \(t\downarrow0\) proves the conclusion without integrability of \(x\).

steps.title: Integrability of bounded exponential tests
steps.body:
If \(|f|\le B\), then \(tf\le |t|B\), so \(0<e^{tf}\le e^{|t|B}\). The right side is an integrable constant under every finite measure. Measurability follows from that of \(f\); integrable domination then proves integrability of the exponential. This establishes the whole real line as the domain of the moment generating function used below.

Boundedness of the test gives \(e^{sf}\le e^{|s|\|f\|_\infty}\). This constant is integrable under the target probability, uniformly for \(s\) in a compact interval, allowing derivatives of its moment generating function.

steps.title: Testing LSI with a normalized exponential tilt
steps.body:
Let \(f\) be bounded and \(C^1\), with \(\| abla f\|\le D\). Put \(M(t)=\int e^{tf}d u\), \(\psi(t)=\log M(t)\), and \(r_t=e^{tf}/M(t)\). Boundedness of \(f\) gives \(0<M(t)<\infty\). Thus \(r_t\) is a positive \(C^1\) probability density relative to \( u\).

Its logarithm is \(tf-\psi(t)\). Differentiation under the bounded exponential integral gives \(\int fr_td u=\psi'(t)\), so

\[H(r_t u\mid u)=t\psi'(t)-\psi(t).\]

This entropy is finite because its integrand is bounded under the tilted probability. The logarithmic gradient is \(t abla f\); its squared norm is at most \(t^2D^2\), so Fisher information is also finite. Applying the log-Sobolev inequality to this density gives

\[2\alpha igl(t\psi'(t)-\psi(t) igr)\le t^2D^2.\]

The finite entropy and Fisher bounds justify this ordinary real-valued inequality for every scalar tilt.

steps.title: The small-tilt entropy quotient
steps.body:
For a \(C^3\) scalar function \(\psi\) with \(\psi(0)=0\), both numerator and denominator of \((t\psi'(t)-\psi(t))/t^2\) tend to zero as \(t\downarrow0\). The product rule cancels the two copies of \(\psi'(t)\), leaving numerator derivative \(t\psi''(t)\); the denominator derivative is \(2t\). On the punctured right neighborhood, their quotient equals \(\psi''(t)/2\). Continuity of the second derivative and one application of l'Hopital's rule prove the limit \(\psi''(0)/2\). The proof explicitly supplies the nonzero denominator derivative and both zero limits.

The constant and first-order terms cancel in \(s\Lambda'(s)-\Lambda(s)\). Its leading term is \(s^2\Lambda''(0)/2\), where \(\Lambda''(0)\) is the variance of the bounded test.

steps.title: A variance bound for bounded differentiable tests
steps.body:
For bounded \(f\), its moment and cumulant generating functions are analytic on all real parameters. The standard second derivative formula at zero is \(\psi''(0)=\int f^2\,d u-(\int f\,d u)^2\), since \(M(0)=1\). This computes the variance limit directly from the bounded exponential tests.

Divide the exponential-test inequality by \(t^2>0\), for \(t>0\), and use the second-order small-tilt entropy expansion. The left side tends to \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}_ u(f)\), while the right side remains \(D^2\). Passing to the limit gives \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}_ u(f)\le D^2\). The boundedness and gradient-bound hypotheses here describe this test function; they are not additional assumptions on the target.

Dividing the tilted LSI by \(s^2\) and taking the small-tilt limit gives \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}(f)\le D^2\). The bounded test class makes this step independent of unknown position moments.

steps.title: Weighted Gibbs integration
steps.body:
Unfold \(\nu=Z^{-1}(e^{-U}dx)\). Scalar multiplication of a measure multiplies its real Bochner integral by \((Z^{-1})\). The weighted-density integral formula then gives \(\int g\,d\nu=(Z^{-1})\int e^{-U}g\,dx\). Continuity of \(U\) makes the weight measurable, and its pointwise value is finite. This equality concerns total integrals; integrability for its later uses is established separately.

The Gibbs change of measure inserts its ordinary positive density into the Lebesgue integral. This is the form in which the weighted derivative identity can be integrated by parts.

steps.title: Weighted Gibbs integrability
steps.body:
Strict positivity of the Gibbs partition follows from differentiability of \(U\); the hypothesis here also excludes an infinite partition. Consequently multiplication of the weighted Lebesgue measure by \(Z^{-1}\) preserves integrability in both directions. The weighted-density integrability equivalence then gives \(g\in L^1(\nu)\) exactly when \(e^{-U}g\in L^1(dx)\). This is the justification for moving the bounded-test integration-by-parts calculation to Lebesgue measure.

The bounded test and gradient bounds, together with finite score energy, control the weighted test-score products. These integrability checks justify the Gibbs integration-by-parts identity on the noncompact state space.

steps.title: The Gibbs integration-by-parts identity for bounded tests
steps.body:
Let \(\psi\) be bounded and \(C^1\) with bounded gradient, and fix a vector \(v\). The directional score \(\langle abla U,v angle\) is integrable by the previously established exponential-moment bound. Therefore the test-score product is integrable. Boundedness of the directional derivative of \(\psi\) also gives its integrability under \( u\).

The Gibbs change of measure makes the three functions \(\psi e^{-U}\), \((D_v\psi)e^{-U}\), and \(\psi D_v(e^{-U})\) integrable under Lebesgue measure. Since

\[D_v(e^{-U})=-e^{-U}\langle abla U,v angle,\]

the global integration-by-parts identity gives \(\int(D_v\psi)e^{-U}dx=\int\psi e^{-U}\langle abla U,v angle dx\). Multiplication by the positive Gibbs normalizer yields

\[\mathbb E_ u\langle abla\psi,v angle=\mathbb E_ u igl[\psi\langle abla U,v angle igr].\]

The weighted integrability conditions justify this identity on the whole state space. No position moment or separately imposed boundary value is used.

steps.title: The sine-score covariance bound
steps.body:
For real \(L^2\) functions \(f,g\), Holder's inequality proves \(fg\in L^1\); their squares are integrable as well. For every real \(c\), integrate \((cf+g)^2\ge0\) to obtain the quadratic \((\int f^2)c^2+2(\int fg)c+\int g^2\ge0\). Its discriminant is nonpositive. Dividing the resulting algebraic inequality by four gives \((\int fg)^2\le(\int f^2)(\int g^2)\). This elementary squared Cauchy-Schwarz form avoids square roots in the compatibility argument.

Center the bounded sine test before applying Cauchy–Schwarz against the centered directional score. The score variance bound and the bounded-test variance estimate then control the square of their covariance.

steps.title: Compatibility of LSI and smoothness constants
steps.body:
Choose \(\|v\|=1\), possible because the space is nontrivial. Put \(s(x)=\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\). The score MGF gives \(\mathbb E s^2\le L\); the bounded Stein identity with \(\psi=1\) gives \(\mathbb E s=0\).

For \(t>0\), use the bounded test \(f_t(x)=\sin(t\langle v,x\rangle)\). Its gradient is \(t\cos(t\langle v,x\rangle)v\), so its norm is at most \(|t|\). The bounded-test variance theorem gives \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}(f_t)\le t^2\). Stein's identity and score centering give \(\mathbb E[s(f_t-\mathbb Ef_t)]=t\mathbb E\cos(t\langle v,X\rangle)\). Squared Cauchy-Schwarz now yields \(t^2(\mathbb E\cos(t\langle v,X\rangle))^2\le L\operatorname{Var}(f_t)\).

Multiply by \(\alpha\ge0\), insert the variance bound, and cancel \(t^2>0\). This proves \(\alpha(\mathbb E\cos(t\langle v,X\rangle))^2\le L\). Dominated convergence applies because cosine is bounded by one and tends pointwise to one as \(t\downarrow0\). Its expectation tends to one, proving \(\alpha\le L\). No integrability of \(X\) itself is needed.

For the unit direction, the derivative of the sine test is \(t\cos(t\langle v,x\rangle)\). Cancelling the positive factor \(t^2\) gives the cosine inequality, and bounded convergence sends its expectation to one.

steps.title: The positive-dimensional compatibility conclusion
steps.body:
This result removes two temporary restrictions from the previous proof. If \(\alpha<0\), then \(\alpha\le0\le L\) immediately. Otherwise, LSI includes the assertion that the Gibbs law is a probability measure. An infinite partition would make its normalizing scalar zero and hence make the Gibbs measure zero, contradicting mass one. Thus the partition is finite, and the nonnegative-constant compatibility theorem applies. The final hypotheses are precisely LSI, differentiability, Lipschitz gradient, finite dimension, and a nontrivial state space.

In positive dimension a unit vector exists, so the preceding directional argument proves \(\alpha\le L\). In the singleton case no unit direction is available; the final entropy theorem handles that case directly with zero KL.

sections.title: The gradient second moment from finite relative entropy
sections.intro:
Assume the Gibbs potential is differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(L>0\), and the Gibbs law is normalized. Its directional score exponential-moment estimate implies \(\int e^{\| abla U\|^2/(4L)}d u\le2^{d/2}\le e^{d/2}\). To prove this, average the directional inequality against an auxiliary radial Gaussian and evaluate the inner Gaussian integral by completing the square. Tonelli applies before the desired exponential integrability has been established.

The pointwise entropy/exponential Young inequality proves integrability of a nonnegative observable under a finite-relative-entropy law when its exponential is integrable under the reference. Applying its integrated form to \(\| abla U\|^2/(4L)\) yields \(G_\mu\le4L H(\mu\mid u)+2dL\). If \(0<\alpha\le L\), nonnegativity of entropy permits the coefficient \(4L\) to be enlarged to \(4L^2/\alpha\). No initial position moment or transport inequality is assumed.

steps.title: Convex duality for the entropy integrand
steps.body:
Let \(\Phi(a)=a\log a-a+1\), with its continuous value \(\Phi(0)=1\). For \(a>0\), the elementary inequality \(e^u\ge1+u\), applied to \(u=b-\log a\), gives \(e^b\ge a+ab-a\log a\). Rearranging proves \(ab\le\Phi(a)+e^b-1\). The zero-density case is handled separately: its left side is zero, and its right side is \(e^b\ge0\). Thus this entropy/exponential Young inequality remains valid at zero Radon-Nikodym density.

For \(a\ge0\), convex duality for \(a\log a-a+1\) gives \(ab\le a\log a-a+e^b\). The nonnegative entropy correction controls the negative part at \(a=0\) and supports integrability before optimization.

steps.title: Integrability from finite KL and an exponential moment
steps.body:
Write \(a=d\mu/d u\). Finite KL supplies absolute continuity \(\mu\ll u\) and integrability of the log likelihood; equivalently \(\Phi(a)\) is integrable under \( u\). For a measurable nonnegative observable \(f\), the Young inequality gives \(0\le af\le\Phi(a)+e^f\). Both terms on the right are integrable by the finite-KL and exponential-moment hypotheses.

Domination proves \(af\in L^1( u)\). The Radon-Nikodym weighted-integrability equivalence then gives \(f\in L^1(\mu)\). In particular, the moment conclusion is derived before any ordinary expectation is manipulated; it is a consequence of the two integrability hypotheses.

Apply the pointwise inequality with the Radon–Nikodym density and the nonnegative observable. Finite KL and an integrable exponential dominate their product, proving the observable is integrable under the changed law.

steps.title: The entropy variational inequality
steps.body:
Assume \(\int e^f d u\le e^c\). First derive \(f\in L^1(\mu)\) with the preceding theorem. Apply the Young inequality to \(a=d\mu/d u\) and \(f-c\), and integrate: \(\int(f-c)d\mu\le\int\Phi(a)d u+\int e^{f-c}d u-1\).

Probability normalization identifies \(\int\Phi(a)d u\) with the finite relative entropy and \(\int(f-c)d\mu=\int f d\mu-c\). The MGF hypothesis makes \(\int e^{f-c}d u\le1\), canceling the final two terms. Thus \(\int f d\mu\le H(\mu\mid u)+c\), together with the integrability witness used in its derivation. The proof explicitly justifies each weighted integral and subtraction.

Subtract a scalar normalization from the observable before applying the inequality. Choosing that normalization as the logarithm of its exponential moment produces the variational entropy bound with the sharp log-moment term.

steps.title: Integrability of the auxiliary radial Gaussian
steps.body:
For \(b>0\), the real radial Gaussian \(e^{-b\|v\|^2}\) is integrable on every finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. This also follows from the complex Gaussian integrability formula at real positive precision: taking its norm gives exactly the displayed real exponential. This supplies the finite integral needed in the Gaussian linearization argument.

A positive Gaussian precision gives integrable radial decay in finite dimension. This supplies the auxiliary Gaussian averaging measure used to turn directional score estimates into a squared-score estimate.

steps.title: The nonnegative radial Gaussian integral
steps.body:
Let \(b>0\) and let \(d\) be finite. The radial Gaussian \(v\mapsto e^{-b\|v\|^2}\) is nonnegative and integrable. Its nonnegative extended integral therefore equals its ordinary integral, and Gaussian integration gives

\[\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-b\|v\|^2}dv =\left(\frac\pi b\right)^{d/2}<\infty.\]

The expression on the right is strictly positive because \(b>0\). It supplies the finite nonzero normalizing constant for the auxiliary Gaussian average. In dimension zero the empty product is one, so the same formula remains valid. Nonnegativity also permits Tonelli to exchange this Gaussian averaging with the target integral before their final numerical bound is evaluated.

steps.title: Completing the square in an exponentially tilted Gaussian
steps.body:
Complete the square in \(-b\|v\|^2+\langle g,v\rangle\): it equals \(\|g\|^2/(4b)-b\|v-g/(2b)\|^2\). Exponentiating separates the constant factor \(e^{\|g\|^2/(4b)}\) from a translated radial Gaussian. Translation invariance of Lebesgue measure and the radial normalization give \(\int e^{-b\|v\|^2}e^{\langle g,v\rangle}dv=e^{\|g\|^2/(4b)}(\pi/b)^{d/2}\). The identity is proved for nonnegative integrals before any integrability of a random score is assumed.

Completing the square in the auxiliary variable evaluates its exponentially tilted Gaussian integral. The remaining factor is an exponential of the squared norm of the vector paired with it.

steps.title: From directional moment bounds to a squared-norm moment
steps.body:
Suppose \(\mathbb E e^{\langle g,v\rangle}\le e^{L\|v\|^2/2}\) for every direction \(v\). Multiply by \(e^{-L\|v\|^2}\) and integrate in \(v\). Tonelli applies to the nonnegative jointly measurable integrand, so the order of integration can be exchanged without assuming the desired exponential moment in advance.

Gaussian linearization identifies the left side with \((\pi/L)^{d/2}\mathbb E e^{\|g\|^2/(4L)}\). The directional MGF bound controls the right side by \(\int e^{-(L/2)\|v\|^2}dv=(2\pi/L)^{d/2}\). Cancel the positive finite factor \((\pi/L)^{d/2}\) in the nonnegative integral inequality to obtain \(\mathbb E e^{\|g\|^2/(4L)}\le2^{d/2}\).

Average the directional exponential bound against the auxiliary Gaussian. Tonelli applies to the positive integrand, and square completion converts its left side into an exponential squared-norm moment.

steps.title: The exponential Gibbs score moment
steps.body:
The smooth Gibbs score has the previously proved directional MGF bound \(\mathbb E_ u e^{\langle abla U,v angle}\le e^{L\|v\|^2/2}\), obtained from translation invariance and first-order smoothness. Apply Gaussian averaging with \(g= abla U\). This gives a finite nonnegative exponential integral bounded by \(2^{d/2}\); measurability and this finiteness prove ordinary integrability.

Convert the nonnegative integral back to its real expectation. Since \(\log2\le1\), \(2^{d/2}\le e^{d/2}\), giving the convenient bound \(\mathbb E_ u e^{\| abla U\|^2/(4L)}\le e^{d/2}\). Only differentiability, Lipschitz gradient, positive \(L\), and finite Gibbs normalization are used; neither convexity nor LSI enters this exponential-moment theorem.

Choosing the auxiliary variance to match \(4L\) gives the factor \(2^{d/2}\). Bounding \(\log2\le1\) turns its logarithm into at most \(d/2\), which is the dimensional constant needed in the score bound.

steps.title: The gradient moment supplied by finite entropy
steps.body:
Apply the entropy inequality with \(f(x)=\| abla U(x)\|^2/(4L)\) and \(c=d/2\). The Gibbs exponential-moment theorem provides both exponential integrability and the MGF bound; finite initial KL provides the absolute-continuity and entropy inputs. Therefore \(\mathbb E_\mu[\| abla U\|^2/(4L)]\le H(\mu\mid u)+d/2\), with this observable integrable under \(\mu\).

Multiply by \(4L>0\), proving \(G_\mu\le4L H(\mu\mid u)+2dL\) and square integrability of the score. The proof also derives finite Gibbs partition from its assumed probability normalization. The estimate is obtained directly from entropy and Gibbs score exponential moments, without a transport comparison.

Use the observable \(\| abla U\|^2/(4L)\) in the entropy variational inequality, then multiply by \(4L>0\). This yields integrability and \(G_0\le4LH_ u(\mu)+2dL\) simultaneously.

steps.title: The gradient moment in the compatible LSI normalization
steps.body:
If \(0<\alpha\le L\), then \(4L\le4L^2/\alpha\). Finite KL is nonnegative, so replacing the direct estimate's coefficient \(4L\) by \(4L^2/\alpha\) preserves the inequality. Thus \(G_\mu\le(4L^2/\alpha)H(\mu\mid\nu)+2dL\), the coefficient used in the ULA one-step calculation. Integrability is inherited from the stronger direct theorem. The preceding compatibility proof derives \(\alpha\le L\) from the log-Sobolev and smoothness hypotheses in positive dimension.

Because KL is nonnegative and \(\alpha\le L\), the coefficient \(4L\) may be enlarged to \(4L^2/\alpha\). The dimensional term stays \(2dL\), giving exactly the form used in one-step forcing absorption.

sections.title: Spatial differentiability, finite Fisher information, and finite entropy
sections.intro:
For \(t>0\), the frozen Gaussian update has the positive mixture density \(p_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\). Gaussian bounds on a displacement and its square control the component derivative uniformly in its center. Dominated differentiation and dominated continuity therefore prove that \(p_t\) is \(C^1\), even when the initial law is singular and has no position moments.

At observation \(y\), the probability with weight \(K_t(x,y)/p_t(y)\) gives the component-score representation of \( abla\log p_t(y)\). Jensen's inequality and the exact Gaussian displacement moment yield \(\int\| abla\log p_t\|^2d ho_t\le d/(2t)\). If the initial gradient is square integrable, its propagated gradient is also square integrable. The decomposition \( abla\log r_t= abla\log p_t+ abla U\) then proves finite relative Fisher information. Applying the target log-Sobolev inequality with positive constant proves finite positive-time relative entropy.

steps.title: A uniform quadratic Gaussian bound
steps.body:
For \(a>0\), put \(u=a\|z\|^2\). The scalar inequality \(u e^{-u}\le e^{-1}\le1\) gives

\[\|z\|^2e^{-a\|z\|^2}\le a^{-1}.\]

Multiplying the desired bound by \(a>0\) changes its left side to \(u e^{-u}\). The scalar maximum is \(e^{-1}\), attained at \(u=1\), and is at most one. Division by \(a\) gives the displayed estimate. Its independence of the center will control posterior displacement moments without initial position moments.

For \(a>0\), the function \(s\mapsto s^2e^{-as^2}\) is bounded on \([0,\infty)\). This bounds quadratic factors times Gaussian decay independently of the component's center, enabling mixture differentiation without a position moment.

steps.title: A uniform first-order Gaussian bound
steps.body:
The elementary estimate \(r\le1+r^2\), together with \(e^{-ar^2}\le1\) and the quadratic envelope bound, gives

\[\|z\|e^{-a\|z\|^2}\le1+a^{-1}.\]

Multiply \(r\le1+r^2\) by the nonnegative exponential. The constant term contributes at most one and the quadratic term at most \(a^{-1}\). The resulting finite constant is independent of the observation and center, which is the uniform domination needed when differentiating a probability mixture.

The first derivative introduces one displacement factor. Reserving part of the Gaussian exponential bounds that factor uniformly, leaving a constant integrable against any mixing probability.

steps.title: Specify the real Gaussian kernel and its derivative map
steps.body:
With precision \(a\), center \(c\), and the already normalized Gaussian constant \(N_a\), define

\[K_a(c,y)=N_a e^{-a\|y-c\|^2},\qquad D_yK_a(c,y)[v]=-2aK_a(c,y)\langle y-c,v\rangle.\]

The second formula defines a continuous linear functional in the direction \(v\): it is the inner-product functional represented by \(y-c\), multiplied by \(-2aK_a(c,y)\). The next calculation verifies that it is the derivative of the first formula. The ULA specialization is \(a=1/(4t)\).

The derivative map is a continuous linear functional in the observation direction, obtained by pairing with the centered displacement. Defining this functional explicitly fixes the object later integrated over the initial law.

steps.title: Differentiate the kernel by the squared-norm and exponential chain rules
steps.body:
The map \(y\mapsto y-c\) has derivative the identity. The squared-norm derivative is \(v\mapsto2\langle y-c,v\rangle\). Multiplication by \(-a\), exponentiation, and multiplication by \(N_a\) therefore produce exactly

\[D_yK_a(c,y)[v]=-2aK_a(c,y)\langle y-c,v\rangle.\]

These chain rules give a continuous linear map whose value at each direction \(v\) is the displayed expression. Equality at every direction identifies this map with the explicitly defined derivative. This calculation concerns a fixed center and uses no regularity of the potential.

The squared-norm derivative contributes twice the displacement pairing, and division by \(4t\) leaves the coefficient \(-1/(2t)\). Multiplication by the unchanged kernel gives the explicit derivative formula.

steps.title: Find a common integrable bound for all component derivatives
steps.body:
The norm of the inner-product functional \(v\mapsto\langle y-c,v\rangle\) equals \(\|y-c\|\). Hence

\[\|D_yK_a(c,y)\|=2aN_a\|y-c\|e^{-a\|y-c\|^2}\le2aN_a(1+a^{-1}).\]

The construction uses homogeneity of the norm and the operator norm of the inner-product functional, removes absolute values using positivity of \(N_a\) and the exponential, and applies the first Gaussian envelope bound. The resulting constant is independent of both \(y\) and \(c\). A probability mixture therefore integrates this bound without requiring any moment of its center map.

The common envelope depends on positive time and dimension but not on the initial state. Since the initial law has mass one, that constant envelope is integrable for every mixing distribution.

steps.title: The integral of the spatial kernel derivative
steps.body:
For \(c_t(x)=x-t\nabla U(x)\), define the continuous-linear-map-valued integral

\[P'_t(y)=\int D_yK_{1/(4t)}(c_t(x),y)\,d\mu(x).\]

This is the integrated spatial kernel derivative. The symbol here denotes a spatial Fréchet derivative, not the time derivative of the density. The following domination lemmas establish its integrability, continuity, and equality with the spatial derivative of the explicit mixture. Keeping the definition as an integral of linear maps makes each directional evaluation correspond directly to the component kernel derivative.

Integrate the component derivative as a finite-dimensional linear map. Its norm is dominated by the common Gaussian derivative envelope, so this candidate is a finite Bochner integral.

steps.title: Integrate each Gaussian component over the mixing probability law
steps.body:
For a measurable center map \(c\), the function \(x\mapsto K_a(c(x),y)\) is measurable and satisfies \(0\le K_a(c(x),y)\le N_a\). Since \(\mu\) is a probability measure, the constant \(N_a\) is integrable, and so is the kernel.

The calculation starts from integrability of a constant under the mixing probability and uses integrable domination. Its first obligation is measurability, assembled from the center's measurability by composition of the displayed continuous and measurable maps. Its second obligation is the norm bound; positivity removes the absolute value, and the fact that an exponential with nonpositive exponent is at most one supplies the Gaussian peak bound.

At a fixed observation the kernel is bounded by its common peak. Hence it is integrable over the starting probability and its mixture value is finite, as required before differentiating that mixture.

steps.title: Integrate the continuous-linear-map-valued component derivative
steps.body:
The common derivative bound is a finite constant \(2aN_a(1+a^{-1})\). Therefore

\[\int\|D_yK_a(c(x),y)\|\,d\mu(x)<\infty.\]

The proof again applies integrable domination to an integrable constant, now with values in the Banach space of continuous linear functionals. Measurability follows from the explicit derivative formula; the second obligation is exactly the uniform Gaussian derivative envelope. This supplies the Bochner-integrability premise needed to identify the derivative of the mixture.

The linear-map-valued derivative has norm bounded by an integrable scalar envelope. This verifies both its Bochner integrability and the domination needed for the differentiation-under-integral theorem.

steps.title: Differentiate the mixture under the integral sign
steps.body:
For each proposed state \(y\),

\[D_y\!\left(\int K_a(c(x),y)\,d\mu(x)\right)=\int D_yK_a(c(x),y)\,d\mu(x).\]

Dominated differentiation applies because the component derivative is explicit, its norm has a common integrable Gaussian bound, and both kernel and derivative are measurable in the mixing variable. It gives the derivative of the mixture as the integral of the component derivative. Thus mixture differentiability is proved from the kernel, not assumed.

The component derivative formula and common integrable bound satisfy the dominated spatial differentiation hypotheses. Their integral is therefore the derivative of the proposed mixture density.

steps.title: Prove continuity of the mixture derivative with the same domination
steps.body:
For every fixed initial point \(x\), the derivative kernel \(y\mapsto D_yK_a(c(x),y)\) is continuous. Its operator norm is bounded by the same integrable constant for every \(y\). Dominated continuity therefore proves continuity of

\[y\longmapsto\int D_yK_a(c(x),y)\,d\mu(x).\]

Continuity under an integral with a common integrable majorant requires measurability of every section, a common integrable bound, and almost-everywhere continuity of the component map. The preceding lemmas provide measurability and the integrable bound, while the explicit formula and composition of the displayed continuous and measurable maps prove continuity. This continuity is what strengthens mere differentiability to \(C^1\).

At each starting state the component derivative is continuous in the observation. The same bound dominates it near every observation, so dominated convergence proves continuity of the integrated derivative.

steps.title: Combine the derivative and its continuity into a \(C^1\) theorem
steps.body:
A function is \(C^1\) exactly when it has a continuous Fréchet derivative. Apply this criterion to the derivative field \(y\mapsto\int D_yK_a(c(x),y)\,d\mu(x)\).

The integrated derivative field is continuous by the common Gaussian domination. The preceding differentiation theorem identifies it as the derivative at every observation. Together these two facts give \(C^1\) regularity of the mixture for every probability mixing measure, including singular measures.

Differentiability of the mixture together with continuity of its derivative is precisely \(C^1\) regularity. This is stronger than merely continuity of the density and is what the LSI test class requires.

steps.title: Gaussian smoothing of the frozen-drift law
steps.body:
The explicit real density of the update satisfies
