\[p_t(y)=\int K_{1/(4t)}(x-t\nabla U(x),y)\,d\mu(x).\]

The mixture formula follows from the fixed-state Gaussian density and Tonelli. Its exponent agrees with the precision form because \(-\|z\|^2/(4t)=-(1/(4t))\|z\|^2\). Lipschitz continuity of the gradient makes the center map measurable. Since \(1/(4t)>0\), the Gaussian-mixture differentiation and continuity results apply. Hence the density of the specified transition law is \(C^1\).

The frozen-drift law is already identified with this Gaussian mixture. Its density therefore inherits the established \(C^1\) regularity, regardless of whether the initial law itself has a density.

steps.title: The spatial derivative of the mixture density
steps.body:
The derivative field defined earlier equals the spatial derivative:

\[D_yp_t(y)=P'_t(y)=\int D_yK_{1/(4t)}(x-t\nabla U(x),y)\,d\mu(x).\]

The mixture has measurable frozen center \(c_t(x)=x-t\nabla U(x)\). Applying dominated Gaussian differentiation identifies its derivative with the integral of the displayed component derivative. This exact derivative field can then be chosen jointly measurably while retaining agreement with the spatial density derivative.

The spatial derivative of the interpolation density equals the integrated component derivative. This identification lets its score be related to Gaussian component scores in the subsequent posterior calculation.

steps.title: Recover \(C^1\) regularity of the potential from its Lipschitz gradient
steps.body:
The assumptions are differentiability of \(U\) and Lipschitz continuity of \( abla U\). The Riesz isometry identifies

\[DU(x)=\operatorname{Riesz}( abla U(x)).\]

The derivative of the differentiable potential is the inner-product functional represented by \( abla U\). A Lipschitz gradient is continuous, and the identification of vectors with these linear functionals is continuous. Therefore the potential has a continuous derivative and belongs to \(C^1\), with no Hessian assumption.

A globally Lipschitz gradient is continuous, and it represents the derivative of the differentiable potential. Thus the potential is \(C^1\), which supplies the regularity of its positive Gibbs density and reciprocal.

steps.title: The relative density is continuously differentiable
steps.body:
The relative density is \(r_t(y)=Z e^{U(y)}p_t(y)\). The partition factor \(Z\) is constant in space, \(e^U\) is \(C^1\) because \(U\) is \(C^1\), and the Gaussian mixture \(p_t\) is \(C^1\). Therefore \(r_t\) is \(C^1\) at every positive time.

The ordinary product rule combines the constant partition, the continuously differentiable exponential of the potential, and the continuously differentiable Gaussian mixture. The resulting relative density is positive and normalized by the established law identity, so it belongs to the target LSI test class.

The relative density is the product of the mixture density with the positive reciprocal Gibbs density. The product rule gives \(C^1\) regularity, while pointwise positivity and normalization are inherited from the interpolation law.

steps.title: The log-Sobolev inequality for the interpolation law
steps.body:
The log-Sobolev hypothesis states that the normalized Gibbs target is a probability and that its inequality holds for every positive normalized \(C^1\) relative density. The constructed \(r_t\) satisfies each of these test conditions: positivity and normalization follow from the mixture law identity, and \(C^1\) regularity follows from the preceding derivative calculation.

Applying the inequality and then using \(r_t u= ho_t\) gives

\[2\alpha\,H( ho_t\mid u)\le I( ho_t\mid u).\]

Here the entropy and Fisher information are initially nonnegative extended values. This application assumes neither is finite. Their finiteness is established below from the gradient moment and Gaussian score estimate. Thus the original positive-density formulation of the log-Sobolev inequality suffices.

steps.title: Record the square-norm Jensen inequality for probability measures
steps.body:
For a square-integrable random vector \(F\) under a probability measure, convexity of squared norm gives

\[\left\|\int F\,d\mu\right\|^2\le\int\|F\|^2\,d\mu.\]

The norm is convex and nonnegative, and squaring is convex and increasing on nonnegative numbers. Their composition is therefore convex. Square integrability supplies integrability both of \(F\) and of \(\|F\|^2\), so Jensen applies to this convex function on the whole vector space. This general lemma is used under the normalized Gaussian posterior at each proposed state.

For a probability measure, expand \(\int\|v-\int v\|^2\ge0\). This gives \(\|\int v\|^2\le\int\|v\|^2\), the vector Jensen inequality used for the posterior mean score.

steps.title: The conditional distribution of the initial mixture component
steps.body:
At a fixed proposed point \(y\), let \(p(y)=\int K_a(c(x),y)\,d\mu(x)\). The posterior law of the initial component is

\[\lambda_y(dx)=\frac{K_a(c(x),y)}{p(y)}\,\mu(dx).\]

Weight the initial probability by \(K_a(c(x),y)/p(y)\). Positive precision makes the kernel positive and finite, so its mixture denominator is positive. The next calculation shows that this weight integrates to one, establishing the posterior probability before Jensen is applied.

At observation \(y\), weight the initial law by \(K_t(x,y)/p_t(y)\). The denominator is the mixture value, making this a probability describing which initial component contributed to that observation.

steps.title: Prove the real mixture denominator is everywhere positive
steps.body:
Every component \(K_a(c(x),y)\) is positive because its normalizer and exponential are positive. Its support as a function of \(x\) is therefore the whole initial-state space, which has probability one.

The kernel is integrable by its common peak bound. Since it is nonnegative and positive on a set of mass one, its integral is strictly positive. Thus \(p(y)>0\) at every observation, permitting both posterior normalization and a pointwise logarithmic score.

Every Gaussian component is positive and the initial measure has mass one, so \(p_t(y)>0\) for every observation. This allows the posterior denominator and mixture log score to be formed pointwise.

steps.title: Normalization of the component posterior
steps.body:
The total posterior mass equals

\[\int\frac{K_a(c(x),y)}{p(y)}\,d\mu(x)=\frac{p(y)}{p(y)}=1.\]

The kernel is integrable, and the denominator is a positive finite constant for the fixed observation. The normalized kernel is therefore nonnegative and integrable. Pulling the constant \(1/p(y)\) out of its integral gives the displayed cancellation. Hence the weighted measure has mass one and is a probability.

Integrating \(K_t(x,y)/p_t(y)\) in \(x\) gives \(p_t(y)/p_t(y)=1\). Strict positivity and finiteness justify the cancellation, establishing posterior normalization.

steps.title: Prove posterior displacement has finite conditional second moment
steps.body:
The posterior may arise from an initial law without moments. Nevertheless, at each fixed \(y\),

\[\int\|y-c(x)\|^2\,d\lambda_y(x)=\frac{1}{p(y)}\int K_a(c(x),y)\|y-c(x)\|^2\,d\mu(x)<\infty.\]

The quadratic Gaussian bound gives \(K_a(c(x),y)\|y-c(x)\|^2\le N_a/a\). The numerator is therefore a finite integral under the mixing probability. Dividing by \(p(y)>0\) bounds the posterior squared displacement by the finite constant \(N_a/(ap(y))\). Measurability follows from that of the center. This proves posterior square integrability even when the unweighted initial law has no moments.

The Gaussian displacement-square factor times its exponential is uniformly bounded as a function of the center. Dividing its finite initial-law integral by positive \(p_t(y)\) gives a finite conditional second moment.

steps.title: Identify the mixture score as the posterior component-score mean
steps.body:
Dividing the mixture derivative by its positive value gives

\[\nabla\log p(y)=-2a\int(y-c(x))\,d\lambda_y(x).\]

The logarithmic chain rule gives \(D\log p=p^{-1}Dp\). The Riesz identification of linear functionals with vectors commutes with this finite Bochner integral. The component derivative is represented by \(-2aK_a(c(x),y)(y-c(x))\). Pulling out the fixed factor \(1/p(y)\) gives integration against the posterior weight. This proves the score identity at every observation, with all denominators positive and all vector integrals finite.

Divide the integrated gradient identity by \(p_t(y)\). The result is the posterior average of \(-(y-x+t\nabla U(x))/(2t)\), identifying the mixture score exactly.

steps.title: Use posterior Jensen to bound the pointwise mixture score energy
steps.body:
Applying square-norm Jensen to the posterior score identity yields

\[p(y)\|\nabla\log p(y)\|^2\le4a^2\int K_a(c(x),y)\|y-c(x)\|^2\,d\mu(x).\]

The posterior is a probability and its displacement is square integrable, so Jensen applies to the score representation. Multiply that inequality by \(4a^2p(y)\ge0\), substitute the posterior density, and cancel the positive \(p(y)\). The resulting density-weighted inequality can then be integrated in the observation variable.

Apply vector Jensen under the normalized posterior to the component score. Its squared posterior mean is bounded by the posterior mean of its squared norm, with no extra factor two.

steps.title: Compute the exact Gaussian component displacement energy
steps.body:
At precision \(1/(4t)\), the component density is the law of \(c+\sqrt{2t}Z\). Therefore

\[\int K_{1/(4t)}(c,y)\|y-c\|^2\,dy=\mathbb E\|\sqrt{2t}Z\|^2=2td.\]

The affine Gaussian law has the displayed normalized density. Since the standard Gaussian vector is square integrable, pushforward change of variables proves integrability of the density-weighted displacement square as well as its integral formula. The equalities \((\sqrt{2t})^2=2t\) and \(\mathbb E\|Z\|^2=d\) give the value \(2td\).

Conditional on the initial point, the centered displacement is \(\sqrt{2t}Z\). Dividing its squared moment \(2td\) by \(4t^2\) gives component-score energy \(d/(2t)\).

steps.title: Integrate posterior Jensen to obtain the universal smoothing Fisher bound
steps.body:
Integrate the pointwise score inequality, use Fubini, and insert the component displacement moment:

\[\int p(y)\|\nabla\log p(y)\|^2\,dy\le4\left(\frac1{4t}\right)^2\int2td\,d\mu=\frac d{2t}.\]

The component displacement energy has integral \(2td\) for every starting state. Its joint measurability and this constant section integral prove integrability on the starting-state and observation product. Hence the right side of the pointwise Jensen inequality is integrable. The left side is measurable because the positive \(C^1\) mixture has continuous score, and domination makes it integrable. Integral monotonicity and Fubini then justify the computation. The bound requires no initial density or position moment.

Multiply the posterior Jensen inequality by \(p_t(y)\) and integrate in \(y\). The posterior denominator cancels, and Tonelli reduces the upper bound to the exact Gaussian component-score moment.

steps.title: Propagate finite gradient energy without a state second moment
steps.body:
Write

\[ abla U(Y_t)= igl( abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X) igr)+ abla U(X).\]

The first term is in \(L^2\) because Lipschitzness bounds it by \(L\|Y_t-X\|\), and the frozen displacement has finite second moment whenever \( abla U(X)\in L^2\). The second term is in \(L^2\) by assumption. The construction uses the Lipschitz-gradient displacement-energy bound and the \(L^2\) characterization for the discrepancy, adds the pulled-back initial gradient, and transfers the sum to the output measure with the pushforward integral identity for square energies. The initial position cancels from the displacement, which is why no \(\mathbb E\|X\|^2\) premise appears.

The gradient difference is at most \(L\) times displacement, so \(\| abla U(Y_t)\|^2\le2\| abla U(X)\|^2+2L^2\|Y_t-X\|^2\). This uses only a score moment of the initial law.

steps.title: The smoothing Fisher estimate for the update law
steps.body:
The generic mixture Fisher theorem applies with \(c_t(x)=x-t abla U(x)\). Rewriting its integral through \( ho_t=p_t\,dy\) gives

\[ abla\log p_t\in L^2( ho_t),\qquad\int\| abla\log p_t\|^2\,d ho_t\le rac d{2t}.\]

The frozen center is measurable, so the general mixture estimate applies. The identity \( ho_t=p_tdy\) converts integrability of \(p_t\| abla\log p_t\|^2\) under Lebesgue measure to integrability of the score square under \( ho_t\). The same change of measure preserves the integral and its upper bound. The mixture is finite pointwise, so the ordinary density formula is valid everywhere.

The proposal pushforward and mixture density describe the same law. Therefore their Lebesgue-score square integrals agree, transferring the universal smoothing Fisher bound to the law used in entropy production.

steps.title: Retain everywhere positivity for the real density
steps.body:
The extended mixture density is positive and finite at every point for \(t>0\). Consequently its finite real-valued density satisfies:

\[p_t(y)>0.\]

Every Gaussian component is positive, so its mixture against a probability is positive. The common Gaussian peak also makes it finite. Hence \(0<p_t(y)<\infty\) at every observation, justifying the logarithm and reciprocal used in its score.

Pointwise finiteness and positivity are retained when choosing the real representative of the mixture. Hence its logarithm and reciprocal may be differentiated at every observation, rather than only on an unspecified almost-everywhere set.

steps.title: Split the relative score into potential and Lebesgue scores
steps.body:
Since \(r_t=Ze^Up_t\), positivity and finite normalization give

\[\log r_t=\log Z+U+\log p_t,\qquad abla\log r_t= abla U+ abla\log p_t.\]

The partition and mixture are positive and finite, so the logarithm product rule gives the first identity. Spatial differentiability of the positive mixture justifies differentiating \(\log p_t\); differentiability of \(U\) justifies the other nonconstant term. The Riesz identification is linear, so differentiating the sum gives the second identity. The normalization constant has zero spatial derivative.

Since \(\log r_t=\log p_t+U+\log Z\), spatial differentiation gives \( abla\log r_t= abla\log p_t+ abla U\). The constant normalization contributes no gradient.

steps.title: Construct finite relative-score energy from two proved \(L^2\) fields
steps.body:
The potential gradient remains in \(L^2( ho_t)\), while the Gaussian smoothing bound gives \( abla\log p_t\in L^2( ho_t)\). Their sum is therefore in \(L^2\), and the score decomposition identifies it with the relative score:

\[ abla\log r_t\in L^2( ho_t).\]

The proof obtains continuity of the Lebesgue score from \(C^1\) regularity of its positive density, converts the finite Fisher integral to square-integrability, and adds it to the propagated finite gradient energy. The final function extensionality uses the score decomposition \( abla\log r_t= abla\log p_t+ abla U\) pointwise. This is the finite-energy fact used for the bounded logarithmic entropy tests.

The two square-integrable fields are the Lebesgue score and the propagated potential gradient. Their sum has energy at most twice each separate energy, providing finite relative-score energy.

steps.title: Finiteness of relative Fisher information
steps.body:
Square integrability of the relative score implies

\[I(\rho_t\mid\nu)=\int\|\nabla\log r_t\|^2\,d\rho_t<\infty.\]

The squared relative score is integrable under the interpolation law. Its nonnegative integral is therefore finite and equals its ordinary energy integral. This identifies relative Fisher information as a finite number before LSI or entropy production is combined with it.

Integrating the nonnegative squared relative score against the proposed law gives the same finite ordinary energy already constructed. Thus the extended relative Fisher information is finite before any real-value use.

steps.title: Finiteness of relative entropy from the log-Sobolev inequality
steps.body:
At positive time, the constructed density is an admissible LSI test, so \(2\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}(\rho_t\mid\nu)\le I(\rho_t\mid\nu)\). With \(\alpha>0\) and finite Fisher information, the KL divergence must be finite.

The construction uses the target's LSI probability hypothesis, the finite relative-score energy bound, and the target LSI applied to the constructed positive normalized density. If KL were infinity, its product with the positive factor \(2\alpha\) would be infinity. The inequality would then force Fisher information to be infinity, contradicting the proved finiteness. No entropy continuity or initial density smoothness is assumed to obtain this positive-time finiteness.

LSI bounds nonnegative relative entropy by the finite relative Fisher information divided by \(2\alpha>0\). Consequently positive-time entropy is finite, which supplies the finiteness required in the entropy derivative identity.

sections.title: Time differentiation and local space-time integrability
sections.intro:
Let \(g_x=\nabla U(x)\), \(c_t(x)=x-tg_x\), and \(K_t(x,y)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\exp(-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2/(4t))\). At \(t>0\), differentiation of the normalizer and exponent gives \(\partial_tK_t=K_t[-d/(2t)+\|y-x\|^2/(4t^2)-\|g_x\|^2/4]\). No derivative of \(g_x\) is taken.

Assume \(G_0=\int\|g_x\|^2d\mu<\infty\). On a neighborhood of each positive time, a bound by a constant multiple of \(1+\|g_x\|^2\) justifies differentiation under the initial-law integral and proves \(\partial_tp_t(y)=\int\partial_tK_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\). Retaining the Gaussian factor instead gives a bound integrable in both starting point and observation. Its explicit integral proves local space-time integrability of \(\partial_tp_t\) on intervals bounded away from zero. The entropy chain rule uses these estimates after initial gradient energy has been deduced from finite initial relative entropy.

steps.title: The Gaussian normalizer as an explicit time power
steps.body:
The proposal normalizer is defined as the reciprocal of the Gaussian integral. Gaussian Fourier integration evaluates \(\int e^{-a\|z\|^2}dz=(\pi/a)^{d/2}\) for \(a>0\). Substitute \(a=1/(4t)\), simplify \(\pi/a=4\pi t\), and invert the real power to obtain \(N_t=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). Positivity of \(t\) justifies the Gaussian formula and the real-power inversion.

The Gaussian normalizer has time dependence \((4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). Expressing it as a real power separates the positive constant from the time power and permits ordinary scalar differentiation.

steps.title: The time derivative of the Gaussian normalizer
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\). On a neighborhood of \(t\), every time \(s\) remains positive, and the Gaussian integral formula gives \(N_s=(4\pi s)^{-d/2}\). The real-power chain rule therefore gives

\[N_t'=(-d/2)(4\pi t)^{-d/2-1}(4\pi).\]

Because \(4\pi t>0\), the identity \((4\pi t)^{p-1}=(4\pi t)^p/(4\pi t)\) is valid. Substituting \(p=-d/2\) simplifies the derivative to

\[N_t'=-\frac d{2t}N_t.\]

The local equality with the explicit power transfers this derivative to the normalizer defined by the Gaussian integral. Thus the density normalization contributes logarithmic derivative \(-d/(2t)\).

steps.title: The frozen-drift Gaussian kernel
steps.body:
The real component kernel is \(K_t(x,y)=N_t\exp(-\|y-x+tg_x\|^2/(4t))\). The gradient \(g_x\) is evaluated at the initial state \(x\), and is constant when differentiating in \(t\) or \(y\). Its integral over \(y\) is one at positive time by the previously proved Gaussian proposal normalization.

The frozen kernel is the Gaussian density conditional on the initial state. Its center moves linearly with time through the fixed vector \(\nabla U(x)\), while its covariance grows as \(2tI_d\).

steps.title: Its explicit candidate time derivative
steps.body:
Define the explicit candidate derivative \(\dot K_t=K_t[-d/(2t)+\|y-x\|^2/(4t^2)-\|g_x\|^2/4]\). The dimension term comes from the normalizer; the remaining terms come from differentiating the exponent. In the expanded exponent, the mixed inner-product term is independent of time, which explains its absence from this expression. The following theorem verifies that this formula is the derivative.

The derivative field is defined by the explicit normalizer and exponent formula. Naming this function before differentiation makes later measurability and integrability statements refer to one fixed spacetime integrand.

steps.title: Expanding the frozen Gaussian exponent
steps.body:
Set \(z=y-x\). The squared-norm identity gives \(\|z+sg_x\|^2=\|z\|^2+2s\langle z,g_x\rangle+s^2\|g_x\|^2\). For \(s\ne0\), division by \(-4s\) yields \(-\|z+sg_x\|^2/(4s)=-\|z\|^2/(4s)-\langle z,g_x\rangle/2-s\|g_x\|^2/4\). The vector identity and scalar denominator cancellation are proved separately in the proof calculation.

Expanding \(\|y-x+t g\|^2\) and dividing by \(4t\) yields \(\|y-x\|^2/(4t)+\langle y-x,g\rangle/2+t\|g\|^2/4\). The middle term has zero time derivative, simplifying the formula.

steps.title: Differentiating the frozen Gaussian kernel
steps.body:
Write the expanded exponent as \(-A/s-B-sC\), where \(A=\|y-x\|^2/4\), \(B=\langle y-x,g_x\rangle/2\), and \(C=\|g_x\|^2/4\). Its derivative at positive \(t\) is \(A/t^2-C\). The expansion agrees with the original exponent on a neighborhood avoiding zero, so this is also the derivative of the original expression.

Apply the exponential chain rule and multiply by the normalizer. Its derivative contributes \(-dK_t/(2t)\); the exponential derivative contributes \(K_t(A/t^2-C)\). Collecting terms gives exactly its explicit time derivative. No derivative of \(g_x\), and therefore no Hessian, is taken.

Combine the normalizer derivative with the derivative of the expanded exponent. The cross term contributes no time derivative, leaving exactly the stated squared-position and squared-gradient terms.

steps.title: An absolute bound on the kernel time derivative
steps.body:
Put \(r=y-x+tg_x\) and \(e=e^{-\|r\|^2/(4t)}\). The triangle inequality and \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) give \(\|y-x\|^2\le2\|r\|^2+2t^2\|g_x\|^2\). The Gaussian exponential bound gives \(\|r\|^2e\le4t\), while \(e\le1\). Consequently \(\|y-x\|^2e\le8t+2t^2\|g_x\|^2\).

Bound the absolute value of each derivative-coefficient term by their nonnegative sum, multiply by \(e\), and insert these bounds. The resulting upper bound is \(|\dot K_t(x,y)|\le N_t[(d+4)/t+\|g_x\|^2]\). It is uniform in \(y\), and is integrable in the initial variable whenever \(G_0<\infty\). Its purpose is time differentiation under the initial-state integral, and will be replaced by a Gaussian-weighted bound for output-space integration.

Take absolute values term by term in the explicit derivative. Nonnegativity of the kernel allows its factor to be retained, producing a sum of Gaussian-weighted nonnegative energy terms.

steps.title: Measurability of the normalizer
steps.body:
At positive time the Gaussian normalizer has the continuous explicit form \((4\pi t)^{-d/2}\), hence is measurable. Assigning an arbitrary value at zero gives a measurable extension if a whole-time parameter field is desired. Only the positive-time values are used in the Gaussian density and derivative identities.

At positive time the normalizer is continuous, hence measurable. Its reciprocal-power expression also permits a measurable extension when the proof organizes all times in one ambient domain.

steps.title: Joint measurability of the kernel time derivative
steps.body:
Lipschitzness makes \(x\mapsto g_x\) continuous and measurable. Combine this with the measurable normalizer and the explicit algebraic formula for \(\dot K_t\). Products, norms, scalar inverses, and exponentials preserve measurability, giving joint measurability in \((t,y,x)\). This is the input needed to integrate out the initial variable while retaining measurable time-space dependence.

The explicit derivative uses only measurable gradient, norms, scalar operations, and the Gaussian exponential. Their composition is jointly measurable in time, initial state, and observation.

steps.title: The candidate time derivative of the mixture
steps.body:
Define \(\dot p_t(y)=\int\dot K_t(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\). At this point it is an ordinary parameter integral. The subsequent differentiation theorem proves it is the derivative of \(p_t(y)\), and the energy estimates prove its integrability, so differentiation and integrability remain conclusions to prove.

Integrating the explicit kernel derivative over the initial probability defines the candidate mixture time derivative. Its later identification as a derivative requires the uniform integrable bound proved separately.

steps.title: Joint measurability of the mixture derivative
steps.body:
The component derivative is jointly measurable in \((t,y,x)\). Its strongly measurable parameter integral over the probability measure \(\mu\) is therefore measurable in \((t,y)\). This gives a single measurable version of \(\dot p\) for spacetime Fubini and the entropy chain rule.

Parameter integration of the jointly measurable derivative field gives a measurable candidate in time and observation. Absolute integrability, when invoked later, ensures it is also the ordinary integral required by the chain rule.

steps.title: The time derivative of the mixture
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\). Continuity of \(N_s\) gives a neighborhood \(S\) of \(t\) on which \(s>t/2\) and \(N_s<N_t+1\). The derivative bound implies, for every \(s\in S\) and fixed observation \(y\),

\[|\dot K_s(x,y)|\le(N_t+1)\left[\frac{2(d+4)}t+\|g_x\|^2\right].\]

The right side is integrable in \(x\) because \(G_0<\infty\) and \(\mu\) is a probability. The component kernel at \(t\) is also integrable, since it is bounded by \(N_t\). Each component has the time derivative already computed.

Differentiation under an integral with this common integrable derivative bound gives both integrability of \(\dot K_t(\cdot,y)\) and

\[\frac{d}{dt}\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)=\int\dot K_t(x,y)d\mu(x).\]

The integral on the left agrees with the mixture density on the positive-time neighborhood. Hence \(\partial_tp_t(y)=\dot p_t(y)\) at every observation. This argument does not require invertibility of the Euler map or a step-size restriction.

steps.title: Equality of the two Gaussian kernel formulas
steps.body:
The spatial Fisher calculation uses precision notation \(q_a(c,y)=Z_a^{-1}e^{-a\|y-c\|^2}\). Substitute \(a=1/(4t)\) and \(c=x-tg_x\). The normalizers agree by definition, and \(-a\|y-c\|^2=-\|y-c\|^2/(4t)\). This pointwise identity makes the time and spatial calculations use precisely the same normalized Gaussian kernel.

Both kernels have the same Gaussian center and covariance. Substituting their normalizers and exponents proves equality pointwise, allowing spatial and time results developed in the two notations to be combined.

steps.title: A weighted derivative bound
steps.body:
Retain the Gaussian factor instead of replacing it by its supremum. With \(r=y-x+tg_x\), the bound \(\|y-x\|^2\le2\|r\|^2+2t^2\|g_x\|^2\) implies that the absolute derivative coefficient is at most \(d/(2t)+\|r\|^2/(2t^2)+\|g_x\|^2\). Multiplication by \(K_t\ge0\) yields \(|\dot K_t|\le K_t[d/(2t)+\|r\|^2/(2t^2)+\|g_x\|^2]\). Unlike the initial-variable envelope, this bound remains integrable in the output variable.

The weighted bound retains the kernel's Gaussian decay and separates the initial-gradient square from displacement-dependent terms. This is the form suitable for integrating first in the observation.

steps.title: A Gaussian weight controlling the time derivative
steps.body:
Define the nonnegative weight \(\mathcal E_t(x,y)=K_t(x,y)(1+\|g_x\|^2+\|y-c_t(x)\|^2)\). Its three terms correspond to Gaussian mass, initial gradient energy, and Gaussian displacement energy. This weight dominates the derivative with a time-dependent scalar coefficient and can also be reused in spatial integration by parts.

The energy combines one, displacement square, and initial-gradient square under the Gaussian kernel. These are chosen to dominate every polynomial term appearing in the explicit time derivative.

steps.title: Nonnegativity of the Gaussian weight
steps.body:
At positive time the normalizer and the Gaussian exponential are positive, so \(K_t\ge0\). Every term in \(1+\|g_x\|^2+\|y-c_t(x)\|^2\) is nonnegative. Their product is nonnegative; this identifies its norm with itself in the Fubini integrability proof.

Every component is a nonnegative square or constant multiplied by a nonnegative kernel. Their sum is therefore nonnegative, permitting nonnegative Fubini before finiteness is established.

steps.title: The component energy integral
steps.body:
For fixed \(x\), Gaussian normalization gives \(\int K_t(x,y)dy=1\), and the centered Gaussian covariance gives \(\int K_t(x,y)\|y-c_t(x)\|^2dy=2td\). Both integrands are integrable. The initial gradient factor is constant in \(y\), so its integral is \(\|g_x\|^2\). Expand the common energy into these three integrable terms to obtain \(\int\mathcal E_t(x,y)dy=1+\|g_x\|^2+2td\).

For each fixed initial state, integrate the kernel to one and its displacement square using the Gaussian moment formula. The resulting expression depends only on time, dimension, and the initial-gradient norm.

steps.title: Integrability of the Gaussian weight in both variables
steps.body:
The common energy is jointly measurable. For every initial \(x\), its output section is integrable by the component energy theorem. Since the energy is nonnegative, the integral of its norm is exactly \(1+\|g_x\|^2+2td\), an integrable function of \(x\) under the probability law \(\mu\). The product integrability criterion therefore proves \(\mathcal E_t\in L^1(\mu\otimes dy)\).

The initial-gradient square is integrable by the score-energy hypothesis, and all remaining terms are finite constants. The component integral calculation therefore proves integrability of the full pair energy.

steps.title: The integral of the Gaussian weight
steps.body:
Joint integrability allows Fubini, giving \(\int\mathcal E_t\,d(\mu\otimes dy)=\int(1+\|g_x\|^2+2td)d\mu(x)\). Probability normalization and the definition of \(G_0\) reduce this to \(1+G_0+2td\). The displayed equality supplies a finite quantitative bound, in addition to proving integrability.

Integrating the component formula over the starting law replaces the squared gradient by \(G_0\). This gives an explicit finite energy expression, retaining its time dependence for uniform compact-interval estimates.

steps.title: A uniform coefficient on a positive time interval
steps.body:
Set \(C_t=d/(2t)+1/(2t^2)+1\). It is positive for \(t>0\), and is bounded above on any interval \([a,b]\) with \(a>0\) by \(C_a\). This finite coefficient suffices for the local space-time integrability required by the entropy chain rule.

On a positive compact interval, \(t\) is bounded above and \(1/t\) is bounded above by the reciprocal of the lower endpoint. One coefficient can therefore dominate all scalar time factors uniformly.

steps.title: Derivative domination by the Gaussian weight
steps.body:
In the weighted derivative bound, denote the three nonnegative coefficients by \(A=d/(2t)\), \(B=1/(2t^2)\), and \(1\). Each is at most \(C_t=A+B+1\). Therefore \(A+B\|r\|^2+\|g_x\|^2\le C_t(1+\|g_x\|^2+\|r\|^2)\). Multiply by \(K_t\ge0\) to prove \(|\dot K_t|\le C_t\mathcal E_t\).

Multiply that coefficient by the nonnegative Gaussian weight. The pointwise derivative bound then holds throughout the interval with one common integrable function, which is the domination hypothesis for the space-time integral.

steps.title: Integrability of the kernel time derivative
steps.body:
The component time derivative is jointly measurable, and its norm is bounded by \(C_t\mathcal E_t\). The common energy is integrable on \(\mu\otimes dy\), and \(C_t\) is a finite scalar at positive time. Domination therefore proves joint integrability of \(\dot K_t\), which licenses the changes of integration order used in the time weak equation.

The energy envelope has finite pair integral and the derivative is measurable. Absolute-value domination consequently proves integrability of the kernel time derivative under the Gaussian pair measure.

steps.title: Spatial integrability of the mixture derivative
steps.body:
Fubini applied to the jointly integrable component derivative first gives \(\dot p_t\in L^1(dy)\). The norm inequality for Bochner integration gives \(|\dot p_t(y)|\le\int|\dot K_t(x,y)|d\mu(x)\). Integrate in \(y\), exchange the two integrals, and dominate by \(C_t\mathcal E_t\). The exact envelope integral yields \(\int|\dot p_t(y)|dy\le C_t(1+G_0+2td)\).

The norm of the mixture derivative is at most the mixture of the kernel derivative norms. Fubini and the finite pair bound therefore give spatial integrability after the initial state is averaged out.

steps.title: Spacetime integrability of the mixture derivative
steps.body:
Joint measurability of \(\dot p\) permits the product integrability criterion on \([a,b]\times E\), where \(a>0\). Every time section is in \(L^1(dy)\). For times in the interval, \(C_t\le C_a\) and \(1+G_0+2td\le1+G_0+2bd\), giving the common finite scalar bound \(\int|\dot p_t|dy\le C_a(1+G_0+2bd)\). The time interval has finite measure, so the section norms are integrable. Hence \(\dot p\in L^1(dt\,dy)\) locally away from zero. If \(a>b\), the restricted time measure is zero and the same argument remains valid.

The uniform compact-time coefficient and the energy integral provide an integrable time majorant. Integrating that majorant over the finite interval proves the full spacetime \(L^1\) estimate used by bounded entropy calculus.

sections.title: Jointly measurable densities and relative scores
sections.intro:
The Gaussian kernel and its explicit spatial derivative are jointly measurable in positive time, starting point, and observation. Parameter integration gives jointly measurable mixture densities and derivative fields. This is the measurability needed for the subsequent space-time integrals.

At positive time the density is everywhere positive. Dividing its gradient by the density and adding \(\nabla U\) yields one jointly measurable relative score field, equal pointwise to \(\nabla\log r_t\). A separately assigned value at time zero or negative times changes none of the integrals over positive time.

steps.title: Integrate a jointly measurable Gaussian kernel
steps.body:
The density is a nonnegative parameter integral \(p_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\). The normalizer, affine center, norm, and exponential are measurable in \((t,y,x)\). The parameterized nonnegative integral is therefore measurable. Passing from the extended integral to its real value preserves measurability. Multiplication by \(Z e^{U(y)}\) gives the joint measurability of \(r_t(y)\).

The explicit positive-time formulas give one jointly measurable family on the domain \((0,\infty)\times E\). If a value at zero is needed to define an ambient spacetime field, it may be assigned separately on that measurable time slice. No choice at zero affects any positive-time density identity or spacetime integral.

The Gaussian kernel is a composition of measurable algebraic operations with the continuous exponential. Parameter integration preserves joint measurability in the remaining time and observation variables.

steps.title: Measurability of the spatial derivative
steps.body:
The derivative kernel is a continuous linear functional proportional to the inner product with the Gaussian residual:

\[D_yK_t(x,y)[v]=-\frac{K_t(x,y)}{2t}\langle y-x+t\nabla U(x),v\rangle.\]

The inner-product-to-dual map is continuous, so this is jointly strongly measurable as a continuous-linear-map-valued function. Its Bochner integral in \(x\), denoted \(A_t(y)\), remains strongly measurable. At positive times the earlier differentiation theorem identifies \(A_t=D p_t\).

The explicit spatial derivative is the kernel times a linear displacement functional. Its joint measurability and finite-dimensional coordinate integration yield a measurable mixture derivative field.

steps.title: One relative-score field for all spacetime integrals
steps.body:
Define

\[\mathcal S(t,y)= abla U(y)+p_t(y)^{-1}\mathcal R^{-1}(A_t(y)),\]

where \(\mathcal R^{-1}\) is the inverse Riesz identification of the continuous dual with the Hilbert space. Continuous scalar multiplication, inversion as a measurable real function, and the previous measurability results make \(\mathcal S\) jointly strongly measurable.

For \(t>0\), \(p_t>0\), so the log chain rule and \(r_t=Z e^U p_t\) give

\[\mathcal S(t,y)= abla U(y)+ abla\log p_t(y)= abla\log r_t(y).\]

Thus the measurable field is the relative score wherever it is used. Its auxiliary extension at nonpositive time introduces no analytic premise into the proof.

Dividing the mixture gradient by its strictly positive density defines one jointly measurable Lebesgue score. Adding the continuous potential gradient gives the relative score field used uniformly throughout positive-time spacetime integrals.

sections.title: The Gaussian weak equation for bounded finite-energy tests
sections.intro:
Write \(g(x)= abla U(x)\), \(c_t(x)=x-tg(x)\), and \(K_t(x,y)=N_t e^{-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2/(4t)}\). For fixed starting point, the spatial flux is \(F_{t,x}= abla_yK_t+K_tg(x)\). Direct coordinate differentiation and an orthonormal-basis sum prove \(\operatorname{div}_yF_{t,x}=\dot K_t\). This agrees with diffusion coefficient one and drift \(-g(x)\).

Let \(\psi\) be bounded and \(C^1\), with \( abla\psi\in L^2( ho_t)\), and assume finite initial gradient energy. Gaussian second moments and Cauchy–Schwarz prove integrability of the flux-test product, the flux-gradient product, and the flux derivative times the test. Global coordinate integration by parts is therefore valid. Summing coordinates and using Fubini yields \(\int\dot p_t\psi\,dy=-\iint\langle F_{t,x}, abla\psi angle d\mu\,dy\). The equation follows from the explicit Gaussian kernel; no Hessian of the potential or assumed weak equation is used.

steps.title: Choose the spatial flux with the correct Fokker–Planck sign
steps.body:
The component density evolves under frozen drift \(-g(x)\). Its time derivative is \(\Delta_yK_t+\operatorname{div}_y(K_tg(x))\), so define

\[F_{t,x}(y)=\nabla_yK_t(x,y)+K_t(x,y)g(x)=K_t(x,y)\left(g(x)-\frac{y-c_t(x)}{2t}\right).\]

The last expression defines this flux. Its divergence equals the density's time derivative, while the weak equation consequently carries a minus sign after integration by parts. The frozen gradient \(g(x)\) is constant in the spatial variable \(y\), which avoids differentiating the possibly merely Lipschitz gradient field.

The flux uses the frozen starting gradient \(\nabla U(x)\), not the current gradient at the observation. Its divergence equals the kernel time derivative, while the difference from the target drift later appears as entropy forcing.

steps.title: Differentiate each coordinate of the flux explicitly
steps.body:
Let \(r=y-c_t(x)\). For a direction \(v\), differentiating the kernel and the affine residual gives

\[D_v\langle F_{t,x}(y),v\rangle=K_t(x,y)\left(\frac{\langle r,v\rangle^2}{4t^2}-\frac{\langle r,v\rangle\langle g(x),v\rangle}{2t}-\frac{\|v\|^2}{2t}\right).\]

The affine vector factor has derivative \(-v/(2t)\) in direction \(v\). Pairing with the fixed \(v\) contributes \(-\|v\|^2/(2t)\). The product rule contributes the derivative of the kernel times \(\langle g-r/(2t),v\rangle\). Inserting \(D_vK_t=-K_t\langle r,v\rangle/(2t)\) and expanding gives the other two terms. The frozen \(g(x)\) is constant in \(y\), so no second derivative of the potential is taken.

Differentiate each flux component using the Gaussian gradient and product rules. The resulting diagonal quadratic displacement and drift terms are the coordinate contributions to its divergence.

steps.title: Sum the directional derivatives to obtain a coordinate-free divergence
steps.body:
Sum over an orthonormal basis \((b_i)_{i=1}^d\). Parseval gives \(\sum_i\langle r,b_i\rangle^2=\|r\|^2\), completeness gives \(\sum_i\langle r,b_i\rangle\langle g,b_i\rangle=\langle r,g\rangle\), and \(\sum_i\|b_i\|^2=d\). Thus

\[\operatorname{div}F_{t,x}=K_t\left(-\frac d{2t}+\frac{\|r\|^2}{4t^2}-\frac{\langle r,g\rangle}{2t}\right)=K_t\left(-\frac d{2t}+\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{4t^2}-\frac{\|g\|^2}{4}\right).\]

For the last equality substitute \(r=y-x+tg\) and expand its squared norm. Its mixed term cancels the displayed pairing with \(g\), leaving the squared-position and squared-gradient terms. Positive time justifies the denominator operations. The resulting coefficient is the same one obtained by differentiating the kernel in time.

Summing over an orthonormal coordinate basis collects displacement squares into a Euclidean squared norm and diagonal constants into the dimension. This gives a coordinate-free divergence formula.

steps.title: The density of the initial/output pair
steps.body:
The pair \((X,Y_t)\), constructed from independent initial state and standard noise, satisfies

\[\mathcal L(X,Y_t)(dx,dy)=K_t(x,y)\,\mu(dx)\,dy.\]

The identity for the conditional Gaussian starting-proposal pair-density formula already proves this transport for a measurable center map. Apply it to \(x\mapsto x-t\nabla U(x)\), whose measurability follows from the Lipschitz gradient. It then checks that the real kernel here is exactly the previously normalized proposal density. This identity transfers integrability proved on the independent initial/noise probability to the kernel-weighted integrals used in integration by parts.

The independent state-noise pair is pushed to the starting-proposal pair. Its conditional Gaussian density is the kernel, so nonnegative and integrable pair expectations have the stated Lebesgue representation.

steps.title: Prove flux pairings integrable by transporting two \(L^2\) factors
steps.body:
For a continuous scalar field \(\varphi\in L^2(\rho_t)\), the coordinate flux pairing is integrable:

\[\int K_t(x,y)\left|\left\langle g(x)-\frac{y-c_t(x)}{2t},v\right\rangle\varphi(y)\right|\,d\mu(x)\,dy<\infty.\]

Under the independent pair \((X,Z)\), the vector factor is \(g(X)-(\sqrt{2t}/(2t))Z\). Both terms are in \(L^2\), by finite initial gradient energy and the Gaussian second moment. Its pairing with fixed \(v\) is therefore in \(L^2\). Pushforward change of variables gives \(\varphi(Y_t)\in L^2\). Cauchy–Schwarz proves integrability of their scalar product. The pair-density identity gives the displayed weighted Lebesgue integral, without a pointwise decay assumption on the test.

The flux pairing can be transported to a product of square-integrable fields on the independent-noise source. Cauchy–Schwarz proves absolute integrability there and hence in the kernel representation.

steps.title: Admit the gradient pairing of a \(C^1\) finite-energy test
steps.body:
Choose the scalar field \(\varphi(y)=D\psi(y)[v]=\langle abla\psi(y),v angle\). For \(\psi\in C^1\), this field is continuous. If \( abla\psi\in L^2( ho_t)\), its coordinate pairing is also in \(L^2\).

For a fixed direction \(v\), the derivative of the \(C^1\) test is \(D\psi(y)[v]=\langle abla\psi(y),v angle\), a continuous function. Its absolute value is bounded by \(\|v\|\| abla\psi(y)\|\), so it has finite square energy. The flux-pairing estimate then gives the required integrability of \(F_i\partial_i\psi\).

A bounded \(C^1\) test with finite gradient square energy lies in the intended weak-test class. The preceding flux estimate verifies integrability of its gradient pairing before integration by parts.

steps.title: Control the boundary product from boundedness of the test
steps.body:
A bounded continuous test satisfies \(|\psi|\le M\), hence belongs to \(L^2(\rho_t)\) because \(\rho_t\) is a probability measure. The general flux-pairing result therefore gives integrability of \(\langle F_{t,x}(y),v\rangle\psi(y)\).

A bounded test has finite square energy under the interpolation probability. Pair it with the finite-energy flux by Cauchy–Schwarz to obtain integrability of \(F_i\psi\), the boundary product required for global integration by parts. No separate pointwise decay of the test at infinity is assumed.

The test itself is bounded, so multiplying by an integrable flux component preserves integrability. This supplies the boundary-product condition in the global coordinate integration-by-parts theorem.

steps.title: Match the divergence to the independently differentiated Gaussian kernel
steps.body:
Direct differentiation of the normalized Gaussian kernel gives its time derivative:

\[\dot K_t(x,y)=K_t(x,y)\left(-\frac d{2t}+\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{4t^2}-\frac{\|\nabla U(x)\|^2}{4}\right).\]

Summing the coordinate flux derivatives gives the same scalar expression as the kernel time derivative. The identity follows by expanding the centered displacement square and canceling its mixed terms. Thus the weak PDE uses a proved equality of explicit derivatives, rather than an assumed evolution equation.

The divergence and time derivative have been calculated independently from their explicit formulas. Algebraic comparison identifies them pointwise, fixing both the diffusion and drift signs in the weak equation.

steps.title: Dominate each unit-coordinate flux derivative by a quadratic Gaussian energy
steps.body:
For \(\|v\|=1\), Cauchy–Schwarz bounds \(|\langle r,v\rangle|\le\|r\|\) and \(|\langle g,v\rangle|\le\|g\|\). The inequality \(\|r\|\|g\|\le\|r\|^2+\|g\|^2\) then gives

\[\left|D_v\langle F_{t,x},v\rangle\right|\le\left(\frac1{4t^2}+\frac1{2t}\right)K_t(x,y)(1+\|g(x)\|^2+\|r\|^2).\]

Apply the triangle inequality to the three coordinate derivative terms. The squared pairing is bounded by \(\|r\|^2\), and the mixed pairing is bounded by \(\|r\|\|g\|\le\|r\|^2+\|g\|^2\). Each resulting scalar coefficient is bounded by the sum \(1/(4t^2)+1/(2t)\). Multiplying by \(K_t\ge0\) gives the displayed inequality. Only quadratic gradient energy is required.

A derivative of one flux coordinate is bounded by the kernel times a constant plus quadratic displacement and gradient energies. These are precisely the terms included in the established Gaussian energy envelope.

steps.title: Integrability of the coordinate flux derivatives
steps.body:
The common envelope \(K_t(1+\|g(X)\|^2+\|Y-c_t(X)\|^2)\) is jointly integrable: its integral is \(1+G_0+2td\), where \(G_0=\int\|\nabla U\|^2d\mu\). The preceding pointwise bound therefore proves joint integrability of every unit-coordinate flux derivative.

The explicit polynomial-Gaussian derivative formula is jointly measurable because the gradient and the elementary kernel operations are measurable. Its absolute value is bounded by a finite time coefficient times the Gaussian weight just integrated. Domination therefore proves absolute integrability of the coordinate derivative, as required before Fubini and integration by parts.

Integrating the quadratic envelope first in the Gaussian observation and then in the initial law gives a finite value from dimension and \(G_0\). This verifies absolute integrability of each coordinate derivative.

steps.title: Apply global integration by parts after proving all three product integrabilities
steps.body:
For one unit coordinate \(v\), global integration by parts gives

\[\int D_v\langle F_{t,x}(y),v\rangle\,\psi(y)\,d\mu(x)\,dy=-\int\langle F_{t,x}(y),v\rangle D_v\psi(y)\,d\mu(x)\,dy.\]

The coordinate derivative times the bounded test is integrable by derivative domination. The flux times the directional test derivative is integrable by the finite-gradient-energy pairing estimate, and the flux times the test is integrable by boundedness. Fubini provides these three section conditions for almost every initial state. At such a state both functions are differentiable, so global directional integration by parts applies. Integrating its section identity over the initial law gives the displayed equality. The required condition at infinity is integrability of these products; no additional pointwise test decay is assumed.

The product, its directional derivative, and the flux-gradient pairing are all integrable. These checks make global integration by parts applicable without assuming compact support of the bounded test.

steps.title: The weak equation for bounded continuously differentiable tests
steps.body:
Sum the coordinate identities over an orthonormal basis. The divergence identity turns the sum on the left into \(\dot K_t\), while completeness of the basis turns the sum on the right into \(\langle F_{t,x},\nabla\psi\rangle\). Fubini then yields

\[\int\dot p_t(y)\psi(y)\,dy=-\int\langle F_{t,x}(y),\nabla\psi(y)\rangle\,d\mu(x)\,dy.\]

Each coordinate integrand is integrable by the preceding estimates, so finite sums commute with their integrals. The time derivative of the kernel is integrable, and multiplication by the bounded test preserves that property. Fubini consequently exchanges the starting-state and observation integrals and identifies their mixture with \(\dot p_t\). All integrability conditions follow from the Gaussian law, initial gradient energy, boundedness of the test, and finite test-gradient energy.

Sum the coordinate identities and use divergence equal to the kernel time derivative. Fubini identifies the mixture derivative on the left, producing the weak equation for every admitted bounded finite-energy test.

sections.title: Relative Fisher information and the frozen-gradient discrepancy
sections.intro:
Let \( ho_t\) be the frozen Gaussian interpolation, \(r_t=d ho_t/d u\), \(s_t= abla\log r_t\), and \(G_0=\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu<\infty\). The decomposition \(s_t= abla\log p_t+ abla U\), the Gaussian score estimate, and the propagated gradient moment give

\[I_t\le4(1+L^2t^2)G_0+8tdL^2+d/t.\]

This estimate is uniformly finite on positive compact time intervals and proves local space-time integrability of \(r_t\|s_t\|^2\) under \(dt\,d u\). The same intervals have integrable frozen-gradient discrepancy, with the bound \(\mathbb E\| abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). Changing variables to the initial/output pair law gives the identical bound with Gaussian kernel weight. These two energies justify the score pairings and removal of bounded-log tests.

steps.title: A square bound for the sum of two vectors
steps.body:
The triangle inequality gives \(\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|\). Square both nonnegative sides and use \(2\|x\|\|y\|\le\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2\), which follows from \((\|x\|-\|y\|)^2\ge0\). This proves \(\|x+y\|^2\le2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2\), the pointwise estimate used to split relative Fisher energy.

Expand \(\|a+b\|^2\), bound the mixed term by \(2\|a\|\|b\|\), and use \(2uv\le u^2+v^2\). This gives the factor two without requiring any relation between the vectors.

steps.title: Splitting the relative-score energy
steps.body:
The jointly measurable score field agrees at positive time with the relative score. Its decomposition is \(s_t= abla U+ abla\log p_t\). The propagated gradient is square integrable, and Gaussian smoothing gives \(\mathbb E_{ ho_t}\| abla\log p_t\|^2\le d/(2t)\). These facts also prove integrability of the relative-score square.

Apply the squared sum bound pointwise and integrate: \(I_t\le2G_t+2\mathbb E_{ ho_t}\| abla\log p_t\|^2\le2G_t+d/t\). The proof keeps the integrability witnesses for all terms before using integral monotonicity.

Split the relative score into the Lebesgue score and potential gradient. The preceding square inequality bounds its energy by twice each component energy, which are estimated by Gaussian smoothing and propagated score moments.

steps.title: An explicit finite relative-score energy bound
steps.body:
The interpolation gradient-moment estimate is \(G_t\le2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2\). Substitute it into \(I_t\le2G_t+d/t\) and distribute the factor two. This gives \(I_t\le4(1+L^2t^2)G_0+8tdL^2+d/t\). Every quantity on the right is determined by the initial gradient energy and the original potential; no entropy-production assumption is used.

Insert the Gaussian Fisher bound \(d/(2t)\) and the propagated gradient estimate. The result is finite at each positive time and uniformly integrable on intervals bounded away from zero.

steps.title: The weighted density representation of score energy
steps.body:
The explicitly constructed relative density satisfies \(r_t u= ho_t\). The weighted-density integrability equivalence therefore transports integrability of \(\|s_t\|^2\) under \( ho_t\) to integrability of \(r_t\|s_t\|^2\) under the fixed target \( u\). The corresponding integral identity is \(\int r_t\|s_t\|^2d u=\int\|s_t\|^2d ho_t\). Strict positivity and measurability of the constructed density justify the ordinary weighted-integral formulas.

Changing from the proposed law to its density multiplies the score square by \(p_t\), or by \(r_t\) under Gibbs. These are equivalent representations of the same finite energy.

steps.title: Spacetime integrability of relative-score energy
steps.body:
The relative density and the chosen relative-score field are jointly measurable in time and space. Their weighted energy is nonnegative. On a positive interval \([a,b]\), the section at every time is integrable by the density-change theorem.

Since \(0<a\le t\le b\), the quantitative estimate is bounded uniformly by \(4(1+L^2b^2)G_0+8bdL^2+d/a\). The integral of the section norm is exactly its nonnegative energy, so this finite scalar bound makes it integrable in time. The product criterion yields \(r_t\|s_t\|^2\in L^1(dt\,d\nu)\) on the interval. This is the spacetime dominating function required to pass from bounded entropy tests to the full relative Fisher term.

The explicit time bound is a sum of powers of time and \(1/t\). On a positive compact interval each is integrable, proving spacetime square integrability of the measurable relative-score field.

steps.title: The frozen-gradient discrepancy on the independent-noise space
steps.body:
For the fixed independent pair \((X,Z)\sim\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)\), define \(e_t(X,Z)= abla U(X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z)- abla U(X)\). The underlying probability space is independent of time. This avoids assuming a jointly measurable choice of a state-space conditional expectation when integrating the error energy over time.

The discrepancy is evaluated at the independent-noise proposal and its initial state. Its measurability follows from the continuous gradient and update map, fixing one field for subsequent pair integrals.

steps.title: Spacetime integrability of discrepancy energy
steps.body:
The proposal and Lipschitz gradient make \((t,X,Z)\mapsto\|e_t(X,Z)\|^2\) jointly measurable. For \(t\ge0\), the exact Gaussian calculation already gives integrability and \(\mathbb E\|e_t\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). On a compact nonnegative time interval this is at most \(L^2(b^2G_0+2bd)\). The time measure is finite, so Fubini's integrability criterion proves the squared error is integrable on the time/initial-state/noise product.

The pointwise gradient Lipschitz estimate bounds its square by \(L^2\) times displacement square. The exact displacement formula is polynomial in time with finite coefficients, giving an integrable spacetime energy.

steps.title: The gradient-error energy under the Gaussian pair law
steps.body:
Map the independent initial/noise pair by \(T_t(x,z)=(x,x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z)\). The squared error as a function of the output pair is \(F(x,y)=\| abla U(y)- abla U(x)\|^2\). Its composition with \(T_t\) is exactly the frozen-gradient discrepancy from the Gaussian energy calculation. Measurability of \(T_t\) and continuity of \(F\) let the map-measure integrability and integral theorems transport both the integrability witness and the bound \(L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\) to the initial/output pair law.

The pair-law change of variables transports the discrepancy energy from independent noise to the Gaussian starting-observation pair. Because the integrand is nonnegative, the identity can be established before signed Fubini is needed.

steps.title: The kernel representation of gradient-error energy
steps.body:
The pair law is identified with \(K_t(x,y)\,\mu(dx)dy\) by the previously proved Gaussian proposal pair-density theorem. The proof specializes its measurable center to \(x-t abla U(x)\); the precision and step-size versions of the kernel agree pointwise.

Rewrite the pair-law energy theorem using this exact density identity. The weighted-density integrability equivalence gives \(K_t\| abla U(y)- abla U(x)\|^2\in L^1(\mu\otimes dy)\), and its integral formula gives the sharp bound \(\int K_t\| abla U(y)- abla U(x)\|^2d\mu\,dy\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). The change of measure preserves the constants in this error-energy bound, which are used in the entropy recurrence.

Rewriting the pair measure using its conditional Gaussian density gives the kernel-weighted energy. Thus the same sharp bound is available in the weak PDE's Lebesgue integral representation.

sections.title: Bounded logarithmic tests and entropy primitives
sections.intro:
For \(M=m+1\), define \(\chi_m(z)=M\arctan(z/M)\) and \(w_m(z)=(1+(z/M)^2)^{-1}\). Then \(\chi_m\) is smooth and bounded, \(\chi_m^{\prime}=w_m\), \(0\le w_m\le1\), and \(|\chi_m(z)|\le|z|\). For each fixed \(z\), the test and its derivative converge to \(z\) and 1 respectively.

For a positive density value \(r\), the primitive \(\Phi_m(r)=\int_1^r\chi_m(\log u)du\) has derivative \(\chi_m(\log r)\), is nonnegative, and is bounded by \(r\log r-r+1\). Its pointwise limit is this entropy integrand. These estimates justify bounded tests in the weak equation, their time chain rules, and dominated convergence to the entropy identity under finite relative entropy.

steps.title: Choose the bounded test and its weight
steps.body:
For a natural number \(m\), write \(c=m+1>0\). Define

\[\chi_m(z)=c\arctan(z/c),\qquad w_m(z)=\frac1{1+(z/c)^2},\qquad\Phi_m(r)=\int_1^r\chi_m(\log u)du.\]

The positive offset in \(c\) prevents division by zero even for \(m=0\). The interval integral is oriented: when \(r<1\), its sign reverses. The formulas define these expressions for every real argument; the entropy claims below explicitly require \(r>0\).

The scale \(M=m+1\) is strictly positive for every allowed index, avoiding a zero denominator. The arctangent bounds the test uniformly in its argument, while the derivative weight remains between zero and one.

steps.title: Differentiate and bound the test
steps.body:
The arctangent chain rule gives \(\chi_m(0)=0\) and \(\chi_m^{\prime}(z)=w_m(z)\). The denominator is at least one, so \(0\le w_m\le1\). The derivative bound implies that \(\chi_m\) is 1-Lipschitz, hence \(|\chi_m(z)|\le|z|\). Independently, \(|\arctan u|<\pi/2\) gives \(|\chi_m(z)|\le c\pi/2\). This last bound controls the time derivative integrand without any log-integrability requirement. Since arctangent has the sign of its argument, \(\chi_m\) does too.

The test is smooth of all orders because arctangent is smooth and \(c>0\). In its first derivative, the factor \(1/c\) from the inner argument cancels the outer factor \(c\), leaving exactly the stated weight.

Differentiating arctangent gives the rational weight \(1/(1+(z/M)^2)\). Its denominator is at least one, proving nonnegativity and the upper bound used to dominate every truncated score energy.

steps.title: Recover the logarithm and its primitive
steps.body:
As \(m\to\infty\), \(z/(m+1)\to0\). The derivative of arctangent at zero is one; its difference quotient therefore gives \(\chi_m(z)\to z\). At \(z=0\) the claim is exact at every index. Continuity of inversion at the positive denominator one gives \(w_m(z)\to1\).

The function \(u\mapsto\chi_m(\log u)\) is measurable and bounded, hence integrable on every finite interval, including intervals containing zero. When \(r>0\), continuity in a neighborhood of \(r\) and the fundamental theorem of calculus imply \(\Phi_m^{\prime}(r)=\chi_m(\log r)\).

For fixed \(z\), the ratio \(z/M\) tends to zero, and \(\arctan u/u\to1\). This gives recovery of the logarithmic test and, after integration in the density variable, its entropy primitive.

steps.title: Dominate the entropy endpoints
steps.body:
We have \(\Phi_m(1)=0\). For \(r\ge1\), both \(\log u\) and its test are nonnegative on \([1,r]\), giving \(\Phi_m(r)\ge0\). For \(0<r\le1\), the test is nonpositive on \([r,1]\), and reversing the interval again gives nonnegativity.

On the positive side, \(0\le\chi_m(\log u)\le\log u\). On the negative side, \(\log u\le\chi_m(\log u)\le0\); reversing the interval preserves the corresponding upper bound for the primitive. In both cases,

\[0\le\Phi_m(r)\le\int_1^r\log u\,du=r\log r-r+1.\]

Pointwise convergence of the test and domination by \(|\log u|\), integrable on the finite interval between 1 and \(r\), prove \(\Phi_m(r)\to r\log r-r+1\). These are exactly the hypotheses for dominated convergence against the finite-KL relative density later.

The entropy integrand \(r\log r-r+1\) is nonnegative and dominates the bounded primitives. For a probability density its integral equals KL, so finite relative entropy supplies the endpoint majorant for dominated convergence.

steps.title: Identify the spatial gradient of the test
steps.body:
For a differentiable scalar field \(f\), the Fréchet chain rule gives \(D(\chi_m\circ f)=w_m(f)Df\). Applying the Hilbert-space identification of linear derivatives with gradients yields

\[ abla(\chi_m\circ f)(x)=w_m(f(x)) abla f(x),\qquad\| abla(\chi_m\circ f)(x)\|\le\| abla f(x)\|.\]

The inequality uses \(0\le w_m\le1\). With \(f=\log r_t\), it supplies square-integrability of the bounded log test gradient from the Fisher information bound.

Applying the spatial chain rule multiplies the relative score by \(w_m(\log r)\). Since this weight is at most one, the gradient's squared energy is bounded by Fisher information, proving admissibility of every bounded test.

sections.title: The integrated chain rule under space-time integrability
sections.intro:
Consider a time-dependent integrand with an integrable initial section, the stated pointwise time derivative, and a jointly integrable derivative on a compact time interval times the spatial measure. The fundamental theorem applied to almost every spatial section and Fubini give the integrated identity for its spatial integral. This also proves integrability of the terminal section.

Applying the identity on every subinterval expresses the spatial integral as a constant plus a primitive of an \(L^1\) time function. It is therefore absolutely continuous and has the integrated derivative almost everywhere. For bounded entropy approximations, endpoint convergence and an integrable bound on their time fluxes permit dominated convergence in the integrated identities. The resulting identity supplies absolute continuity and the almost-everywhere derivative of the full entropy.

steps.title: An integrated identity from a spacetime derivative
steps.body:
Assume \(f(a,\cdot)\in L^1( u)\), \(\dot f\in L^1((a,b] imes u)\), and \(\partial_t f(t,x)=\dot f(t,x)\) for every \(t\in[a,b]\) and almost every \(x\). Fubini gives \(\dot f(\cdot,x)\in L^1(a,b)\) for almost every \(x\). Apply the scalar fundamental theorem to these sections: \(f(b,x)=f(a,x)+\int_a^b\dot f(t,x)dt\).

The time-integrated derivative is integrable in \(x\) by spacetime integrability. The section identity therefore proves terminal integrability of \(f(b,\cdot)\), rather than requiring it separately. Integrate the identity and exchange time and space to obtain \(\int f(b)d u=\int f(a)d u+\int_a^b\int\dot f(t,x)d u(x)dt\).

For almost every spatial point, integrate its time derivative between the endpoints. Spacetime absolute integrability permits Fubini to exchange the two integrations, yielding the integrated identity for the spatial integral.

steps.title: Absolute continuity from spacetime integrability
steps.body:
Apply the integrated fundamental theorem on every subinterval \([a,t]\subseteq[a,b]\). Restricting the spacetime measure preserves integrability, giving both integrability of \(f(t,\cdot)\) and \(F(t)=F(a)+\int_a^t q(u)du\), where \(F(t)=\int f(t,x)d\nu(x)\) and \(q(t)=\int\dot f(t,x)d\nu(x)\).

Fubini gives \(q\in L^1(a,b)\). An indefinite integral of an \(L^1\) function is absolutely continuous; adding the constant \(F(a)\) preserves this property. Equality on the interval transfers absolute continuity to \(F\). Thus regularity of the spatial integral is a conclusion of spacetime integrability and pointwise differentiation.

An integral of an \(L^1\) time function is absolutely continuous. The spacetime norm bound makes the spatially integrated derivative such an \(L^1\) function, supplying this regularity without an assumed entropy derivative.

steps.title: The almost-everywhere derivative of the integrated quantity
steps.body:
The subinterval argument gives \(F(t)=F(a)+\int_a^t q(u)du\) for every \(t\in[a,b]\), with \(q\in L^1(a,b)\). Lebesgue differentiation supplies derivative \(q(t)\) for the indefinite integral at almost every interior time. For each such \(t\), an open neighborhood stays inside \((a,b)\), where the displayed identity holds. The local equality transfers the derivative to \(F\), yielding \(F'(t)=\int\dot f(t,x)d\nu(x)\) almost everywhere. No pointwise derivative assertion at every time, or at the endpoints, is inferred.

The fundamental theorem for absolutely continuous primitives gives the derivative almost everywhere. The exceptional time set has measure zero, which is sufficient for all later integrating-factor inequalities.

steps.title: Passing an integrated identity through dominated limits
steps.body:
Suppose truncated identities have the form \(B_n-A_n=\int q_n d u\). Assume the two endpoint sequences converge to their intended values, \(q_n o q\) almost everywhere, and \(|q_n|\le g\) with \(g\in L^1( u)\). Dominated convergence gives convergence of the right-hand integrals, while the endpoint limits give convergence of the left-hand differences. Their equality for every \(n\) and uniqueness of limits prove \(B-A=\int qd u\).

In the entropy application, the endpoints are truncated entropy integrals and \(q_n\) are bounded-test fluxes on a fixed time interval. Spatial energy estimates supply the pointwise flux limit and a time-integrable dominating bound. This lemma passes the integrated identities to the limit without assuming in advance that the full entropy has already been differentiated.

Pass the approximating integrated identities to the limit in both endpoints and flux. Endpoint domination and spacetime flux domination are checked separately because they use different reference measures and majorants.

steps.title: Regularity supplied by the limiting integral identity
steps.body:
Assume only \(q\in L^1(a,b)\) and the exact identity \(H(t)=H(a)+\int_a^t q(u)du\) throughout \([a,b]\). The primitive of \(q\) is absolutely continuous; adding \(H(a)\) and using the identity proves that \(H\) is absolutely continuous.

Lebesgue differentiation gives derivative \(q(t)\) for the primitive at almost every interior time. The identity holds in an interior neighborhood of each such time, so the derivative transfers to \(H\). This gives precisely the final entropy comparison inputs: local absolute continuity and the flux as derivative almost everywhere.

The limiting identity expresses the function as a constant plus an integral of an \(L^1\) flux. It therefore supplies both local absolute continuity and its almost-everywhere derivative, providing the regularity needed for entropy comparison.

sections.title: The entropy chain rule for the Gaussian interpolation
sections.intro:
Let \(\pi=Z^{-1}e^{-U}dy\), let \(Y_t=X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z_0\) with independent standard Gaussian \(Z_0\), and write \( ho_t=\mathcal L(Y_t)\), \(r_t=d ho_t/d\pi\), and \(S_t= abla\log r_t\). Under the stated potential, log-Sobolev, and finite initial gradient-energy hypotheses, positive-time entropy is finite. Its time regularity is proved by integrating bounded approximations.

For the bounded tests \(\chi_m(\log r_t)\), the Gaussian weak equation and the time chain rule give exact integrated identities on \([a,b]\subset(0,\infty)\). The entropy integrand dominates their endpoints. Half the sum of the frozen-velocity and relative-score energies dominates their fluxes independently of \(m\) and is integrable in time. Dominated convergence therefore yields \(H( ho_b\mid\pi)-H( ho_a\mid\pi)=\int_a^bq(t)dt\). This proves local absolute continuity and derivative \(q\) almost everywhere. The score-pairing identity subsequently writes that derivative as \(-I_t+\mathbb E\langle abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X),S_t(Y_t) angle\).

steps.title: Removing bounded log weights by dominated convergence
steps.body:
Let \(w_m(z)=[1+(z/(m+1))^2]^{-1}\). For a measurable scalar field \(z\) and an integrable field \(f\),

\[\int w_m(z(x))f(x)\,d\nu(x)\longrightarrow\int f(x)\,d\nu(x).\]

The pointwise limit is \(w_m(z(x))\to1\), proved in the pointwise convergence of bounded-log derivative weights to one. Each weighted integrand is measurable, because the weight is obtained by division, squaring and inversion of measurable real functions. Furthermore \(0\le w_m\le1\), so \(|w_m(z)f|\le|f|\). The proof invokes dominated convergence with the integrable majorant \(|f|\). This lemma later removes the truncation from the Gaussian flux, whose two factors are square integrable.

The derivative weights converge pointwise to one and stay between zero and one. Multiplying by the already integrable unweighted pairing gives a common absolute majorant, so dominated convergence removes the weight without changing the reference measure.

steps.title: Why the square-integrable flux pairing is integrable
steps.body:
If \(v,s\in L^2(\nu;E)\), then

\[|\langle v,s\rangle|\le\|v\|\|s\|,\qquad \|v\|\|s\|\in L^1(\nu).\]

Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the integral of the product of the two norms by their finite square norms. The absolute inner product is bounded by this norm product, proving absolute integrability of the pairing. This remains true on the stated measure space without assuming its total mass is finite.

For square-integrable fields \(a,b\), use \(|\langle a,b\rangle|\le(\|a\|^2+\|b\|^2)/2\). The right side has finite integral, proving absolute flux integrability before signed Fubini or limiting arguments.

steps.title: The real Gibbs density and its normalization
steps.body:
Write \(Z=\int e^{-U(x)}\,dx\), and let \(\pi\) be the normalized Gibbs law. Define

\[J(y)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}.\]

The existing probability-mass argument proves \(0<Z<\infty\); differentiability makes \(U\) measurable and gives strict positivity of the partition function. Consequently \(J(y)>0\) at every point. The measure identity is

\[\pi(dy)=J(y)\,dy.\]

The density identity follows from multiplying the unnormalized Gibbs weight by the finite scalar \(Z^{-1}\). Since \(0<Z<\infty\), the resulting measurable function \(J\) is positive and has integral one. The same expression therefore represents the target in ordinary Lebesgue integration; strong convexity is not needed for this change-of-density step.

The Gibbs density is positive and finite pointwise, and its integral is one. Thus \(J\Phi_m(r_t)\) may be read as a Lebesgue representation of the same bounded relative-entropy primitive integrated against Gibbs.

steps.title: The time derivative of the weighted entropy primitive
steps.body:
Let \(p_t\) be the Lebesgue density of the frozen Gaussian update, and let \(r_t=p_t/J\) be its relative density. For the bounded entropy primitive \(\Phi_m\), one has \(\Phi_m'(r)=\chi_m(\log r)\) for \(r>0\). At every positive time, the kernel differentiation result gives \(\partial_t p_t=\dot p_t\), hence

\[\partial_t r_t=Ze^{U}\dot p_t,\qquad \partial_t[J\Phi_m(r_t)]=\chi_m(\log r_t)\dot p_t.\]

The proof applies the time chain rule first to the constant multiple defining \(r_t\), then to the derivative formula for the bounded entropy primitive, then to multiplication by \(J\). The remaining coefficient cancels because \(J(y)Ze^{U(y)}=1\), using the inverse of the strictly positive real partition function and \(e^{-U}e^U=1\). This cancellation is what permits the spacetime estimate to use the Lebesgue \(L^1\) bound on \(\dot p_t\).

Because \(J\) is time independent and \(Jr_t=p_t\), differentiating \(J\Phi_m(r_t)\) gives \(\chi_m(\log r_t)\dot p_t\). This cancellation avoids differentiating the Gibbs density in time.

steps.title: Identifying finite entropy through the chosen density
steps.body:
Let \( u\) be the reference probability and suppose \(\mu=r u\) is a probability measure, \(r\ge0\) is measurable, and \(H(\mu\mid u)<\infty\). Then

\[\mathrm{kl}(r)=r\log r+1-r\in L^1( u),\qquad \int\mathrm{kl}(r)\,d u=H(\mu\mid u).\]

The Radon–Nikodym derivative of \(r u\) relative to \( u\) is \(r\) almost everywhere. Finite KL gives integrability of its logarithm under \(r u\); changing measure makes \(r\log r\) integrable under \( u\). Since \(r\) and the constant one both have finite integral, so does \(r\log r-r+1\). Their probability masses agree, so integrating the last two terms cancels them and gives the stated entropy identity.

The relative entropy is finite at positive time by LSI and the Fisher bound. The density formula therefore identifies it with the ordinary integral of \(r_t\log r_t-r_t+1\), whose mass corrections cancel by normalization.

steps.title: Integrability of every bounded entropy approximation
steps.body:
At \(t>0\), the interpolation has a positive \(C^1\) relative density \(r_t\). Its Fisher information is finite from the initial score moment and Gaussian smoothing; LSI then gives finite relative entropy. The bounded primitive satisfies

\[0\le\Phi_m(r_t(y))\le\mathrm{kl}(r_t(y)).\]

The preceding density lemma proves that the right-hand side is integrable. The left-hand side is measurable: continuity of \(r_t\) and the derivative of \(\Phi_m\) at positive arguments give continuity of their composition. Integrable domination therefore proves integrability for each truncation from this finite entropy majorant. Initial density differentiability, initial Fisher information and a second moment of the state are not required.

The bounded primitive lies between zero and the nonnegative entropy integrand. Finite relative entropy therefore proves integrability of each approximating entropy before its time identity is formed.

steps.title: Convergence of the bounded entropy to relative entropy
steps.body:
For every fixed positive time,

\[\int\Phi_m(r_t)\,d\pi\longrightarrow H(\rho_t\mid\pi).\]

Pointwise convergence \(\Phi_m(r)\to\mathrm{kl}(r)\) holds for \(r>0\). The domination \(0\le\Phi_m(r_t)\le\mathrm{kl}(r_t)\), together with integrability proved above, gives dominated convergence under the fixed Gibbs measure. The density identity \(r_t\pi=\rho_t\), with \(r_t=Ze^Up_t\), identifies the integral of \(r_t\log r_t-r_t+1\) with \(H(\rho_t\mid\pi)\). The limit is therefore the relative entropy of the specified Gaussian interpolation law.

Pointwise convergence of the primitive to \(r\log r-r+1\), together with the finite entropy majorant, gives convergence of both positive-time endpoint entropies. This limit is independent of any time-flux limit.

steps.title: The bounded entropy and its time flux
steps.body:
The two functions used in the time integration are

\[H_m(t)=\int\Phi_m(r_t(y))\,d\pi(y),\qquad q_m(t)=\int\chi_m(\log r_t(y))\dot p_t(y)\,dy.\]

The bounded entropy \(H_m(t)\) uses the fixed Gibbs reference measure; the bounded entropy flux \(q_m(t)\) uses Lebesgue measure. Their different measures match the exact cancellation in the weighted chain rule. The definitions are explicit functions of the mixture density and its kernel time derivative.

The bounded entropy is paired with its explicit time flux on a compact positive interval. Boundedness of the log test lets the spacetime \(L^1\) density-derivative estimate dominate that flux.

steps.title: Admissibility of the bounded logarithmic test
steps.body:
The spatial weak test is \(\psi_m(y)=\chi_m(\log r_t(y))\). Positivity and \(C^1\) regularity of \(r_t\), combined with smoothness of \(\chi_m\), show that \(\psi_m\in C^1\). Its uniform bound is

\[|\psi_m(y)|\le(m+1)\pi/2.\]

The spatial chain rule gives

\[ abla\psi_m(y)=w_m(\log r_t(y)) abla\log r_t(y),\qquad \| abla\psi_m(y)\|\le\| abla\log r_t(y)\|.\]

The test-gradient norm is at most the relative-score norm, whose square is integrable. Continuity of the test derivative supplies measurability. Thus the bounded logarithmic test is \(C^1\) and has finite gradient energy, exactly the conditions required by the Gaussian weak equation.

The test is bounded and \(C^1\), and its gradient norm is at most the relative-score norm. Finite Fisher information therefore places its gradient in the exact finite-energy class admitted by the weak equation.

steps.title: The bounded entropy flux equals the spatial pairing
steps.body:
Let \(K_t(x,y)\) be the Gaussian transition density, \(g=\nabla U\), and \(S_t=\nabla\log r_t\). The proved Gaussian weak equation, applied to the admissible test above, gives

\[q_m(t)=-\iint K_t(x,y)w_m(\log r_t(y))\left\langle g(x)-\frac{y-x+tg(x)}{2t},S_t(y)\right\rangle\,\mu(dx)\,dy.\]

The underlying flux is \(K_t[g(x)-(y-x+tg(x))/(2t)]\). Its divergence equals the kernel time derivative; global integration by parts is justified by the previously proved finite-gradient-energy estimates. Substitute the test-gradient chain rule and the equality between the explicit measurable score field and the relative score. The remaining rearrangement is bilinearity of the inner product and scalar multiplication.

The weak equation converts the time-derivative pairing into the negative spatial flux pairing. Its sign is fixed by integration by parts, and its integrability has been established for this very bounded test.

steps.title: The bounded time chain rule without a spatial time-majorant
steps.body:
On any \(0<a\le b\), the weighted primitive has derivative \(\chi_m(\log r_t)\dot p_t\). The kernel theorem proves \(\dot p\in L^1([a,b]\times E)\), while \(\chi_m\) is bounded by \((m+1)\pi/2\). Thus the derivative of the weighted primitive is jointly integrable.

Integrability at time \(a\) follows from the bounded-entropy lemma after rewriting Gibbs measure as \(J(y)dy\). The generic spacetime FTC/Fubini theorem then yields

\[H_m(b)-H_m(a)=\int_a^b q_m(t)\,dt.\]

Applying the same identity on every subinterval expresses \(H_m\) as a constant plus the primitive of the integrable flux \(q_m\). Thus \(H_m\) is absolutely continuous, and Lebesgue differentiation gives \(H_m'(t)=q_m(t)\) almost everywhere. Boundedness of the test and space-time integrability of the density derivative suffice; no common spatial bound for every time derivative is assumed.

Integrate the pointwise chain rule in time first, using the bounded test to dominate the time derivative. Fubini then yields the entropy endpoint identity without requiring an integrable spatial envelope uniform near each individual observation.

steps.title: Expressing the flux on one independent probability space
steps.body:
Take \(X\sim\mu\) and \(Z\sim N(0,I)\) independently, and set \(Y_t=X-tg(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\). Define

\[V_t(X,Z)=g(X)-\frac{\sqrt{2t}}{2t}Z,\qquad \widehat S_t(X,Z)=S_t(Y_t),\qquad q(t)=-\mathbb E\langle V_t,\widehat S_t\rangle.\]

These fields are defined on the same independent initial-state and Gaussian-noise probability for every time. The frozen velocity is the component spatial flux divided by the positive transition density and evaluated at the proposal.
