Using this fixed reference space makes joint measurability and time domination available for the limiting entropy identity.

The Gaussian pair-law identity replaces kernel-weighted starting-observation integrals by expectations over one fixed independent state-noise probability. This puts all energy and pairing estimates on the same reference space.

steps.title: Square-integrability of the Gaussian flux factors
steps.body:
The initial gradient belongs to \(L^2(\mu)\), and the standard Gaussian noise belongs to \(L^2\). Pulling both to the independent product space and taking their scalar combination proves \(V_t\in L^2(\mu\otimes\gamma)\). The relative score belongs to \(L^2(\rho_t)\). Since \(\rho_t\) is the pushforward of \(\mu\otimes\gamma\) by \(Y_t\), the measurable-map characterization of \(L^2\) gives

\[\widehat S_t=S_t\circ Y_t\in L^2(\mu\otimes\gamma).\]

The initial-gradient and Gaussian moment bounds justify the linear combination defining \(V_t\) in the product \(L^2\) space. The explicit score equals \(\nabla\log r_t\) at positive time, so pushforward change of variables preserves its square energy under composition with \(Y_t\). Cauchy–Schwarz then proves integrability of the inner product of these two fields.

The relative score has finite square energy by the Fisher estimate. The frozen velocity has finite square energy by its Gaussian component and initial gradient, so their flux pairing is absolutely integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz.

steps.title: The exact frozen velocity energy
steps.body:
Independence and the zero Gaussian mean cancel the drift-noise cross term:

\[\mathbb E\|V_t\|^2=\mathbb E\|g(X)\|^2+\frac{d}{2t},\qquad t>0.\]

The proof specializes the already verified affine-Gaussian moment formula with coefficients \(1\) and \(-\sqrt{2t}/(2t)\). The squared coefficient is \((2t)/(4t^2)=1/(2t)\), using \((\sqrt{2t})^2=2t\). This exact finite energy gives a compact-time bound that is uniform away from zero. No moment of \(X\) itself is used.

The frozen velocity consists of the Gaussian component score plus the initial drift. Their mixed expectation vanishes by centered independent Gaussian noise, giving the exact sum of component-score and initial-gradient energies.

steps.title: Transporting the bounded flux to independent noise
steps.body:
The law of \((X,Y_t)\) has density \(K_t(x,y)\) with respect to \(\mu(dx)dy\). Therefore the joint flux identity becomes

\[q_m(t)=-\mathbb E\!\left[w_m(\log r_t(Y_t))\langle V_t,\widehat S_t\rangle\right].\]

The measurable map \((x,z)\mapsto(x,Y_t(x,z))\) has the initial/output pair law as its pushforward. This law has density \(K_t\) relative to \(\mu(dx)dy\). The change-of-variables formula for the integrable weighted pairing therefore equates the kernel-weighted integral with the expectation over the independent product space. Finally \(Y_t-(X-tg(X))=\sqrt{2t}Z\) reduces the residual to the specified velocity field. The change of variables concerns the Gaussian law and does not assume an invariant Euler step.

Changing variables in the bounded flux retains the same state-space test evaluated at the proposal. This lets the derivative weight remain bounded by one while the independent-noise energy majorant is applied.

steps.title: Removing the truncation at fixed positive time
steps.body:
The raw pairing \(\langle V_t,\widehat S_t\rangle\) is integrable by the two \(L^2\) estimates. The scalar map \((x,z)\mapsto\log r_t(Y_t)\) is measurable. Since \(0\le w_m\le1\) and \(w_m\to1\), dominated convergence on the independent probability space yields

\[q_m(t)\longrightarrow q(t),\qquad t>0.\]

The dominating function is \(|\langle V_t,\widehat S_t\rangle|\). This limit is performed after spatial integration by parts; it does not ask for integrability of \(|\log r_t|\,|\dot p_t|\), which is not supplied by the original assumptions.

At a fixed positive time, all factors except the bounded-log weight remain unchanged. Since that weight tends to one and its absolute value is at most one, the integrable full flux dominates the entire sequence.

steps.title: A fixed-reference formula for the relative Fisher energy
steps.body:
Define

\[I(t)=\int r_t(y)\|S_t(y)\|^2\,d\pi(y).\]

The relative-density identity gives \(I(t)=\int\|S_t\|^2\,d\rho_t\). Applying the Gaussian pushforward once more yields

\[\mathbb E\|\widehat S_t\|^2=I(t).\]

The first definition fixes the reference measure for time measurability and spacetime integrability. The equality uses the weighted representation of relative Fisher information and the measurable-map Bochner integral formula. The proof supplies strong measurability of the score norm square explicitly, fixing time in the joint measurable score field.

Pushing the relative-score square through the proposal map expresses \(I_t\) as an expectation on the independent-noise source. This representation is jointly measurable and directly comparable with the discrepancy energy.

steps.title: A uniform bound for every truncated flux
steps.body:
For any vectors \(v,s\) and any \(0\le w\le1\),

\[|w\langle v,s\rangle|\le\|v\|\|s\|\le\tfrac12(\|v\|^2+\|s\|^2).\]

The second inequality is \((\|v\|-\|s\|)^2\ge0\). Integrate on the independent Gaussian space, use the norm inequality for Bochner integrals, and substitute the two exact energies:

\[|q_m(t)|\le\frac12\left(G_0+\frac d{2t}+I(t)\right),\qquad G_0=\int\|g\|^2\,d\mu.\]

The weighted pairing is integrable because \(w_m\) is bounded and both factors are square integrable. The quadratic upper bound is also integrable by those same two energy estimates. Integral monotonicity therefore justifies the displayed estimate for every truncation before a limiting entropy derivative is known to exist.

The absolute truncated pairing is bounded by half the sum of the two unweighted square energies. This bound contains no truncation index and is therefore suitable for both pointwise-time and time-integrated limits.

steps.title: Joint measurability of both time fluxes
steps.body:
The bounded flux is a parameter integral of \(\chi_m(\log r_t(y))\dot p_t(y)\). Both factors are jointly measurable in \((t,y)\), so parameter integration makes \(t\mapsto q_m(t)\) measurable. The raw flux uses the fixed independent space: the map \((t,x,z)\mapsto(t,Y_t)\) is measurable, the explicit relative-score field is jointly strongly measurable, and the velocity field is a measurable algebraic combination of \(g(X)\), \(t^{-1}\), \(\sqrt{2t}\), and \(Z\). Their inner product and its parameter integral are measurable. The definitions at nonpositive times serve only to make these globally specified measurable functions; all analytic conclusions are restricted to positive times.

The chosen score and velocity fields are jointly measurable, and the bounded-log weights are continuous functions of measurable densities. Their products and parameter integrals therefore define measurable scalar fluxes in time.

steps.title: The integrable majorant for the time limit
steps.body:
Fix \(0<a\le b\). The Gaussian energy estimate proves \(I\in L^1([a,b])\). Set

\[D(t)=\tfrac12\left(G_0+\frac d{2a}+I(t)\right).\]

The interval has finite Lebesgue measure, so the constant term is integrable; hence \(D\in L^1([a,b])\). Since \(t\ge a>0\), \(d/(2t)\le d/(2a)\). The uniform flux estimate gives \(|q_m(t)|\le D(t)\) for every \(m\). The fixed-time limit \(q_m(t)\to q(t)\), followed by continuity of the absolute value, also gives \(|q(t)|\le D(t)\). Thus one integrable time function bounds all truncated fluxes and their pointwise limit, as required for dominated convergence in time.

On a compact positive interval, the score and velocity square energies have a common integrable time bound. Their half-sum dominates every truncated flux and the limiting flux, establishing the spacetime dominated-convergence hypothesis.

steps.title: The integrated entropy identity
steps.body:
Let \(H(t)=H(\rho_t\mid\pi)\), represented by the finite relative entropy. For each truncation,

\[H_m(b)-H_m(a)=\int_a^b q_m(t)\,dt.\]

At both endpoints, the spatial dominated-convergence theorem gives \(H_m\to H\). In time, the common integrable majorant \(D\) and the pointwise convergence \(q_m\to q\) give \(\int_a^b q_m\to\int_a^b q\). Uniqueness of limits therefore yields

\[H(b)-H(a)=\int_a^b q(t)\,dt.\]

For the time integral, use Lebesgue measure restricted to \((a,b]\); endpoint singletons have measure zero. The endpoint limits were proved under Gibbs measure, and the flux limit uses the integrable time bound \(D\). These distinct dominated-convergence arguments give the identity without assuming temporal regularity of the full entropy.

Take the truncation limit in the two endpoint values and in the integrated flux separately. Their established dominations then yield an exact identity for the relative entropy between any two positive times.

steps.title: Absolute continuity and the almost-everywhere entropy derivative
steps.body:
The raw flux is measurable and satisfies \(|q|\le D\), so it is integrable on every positive-time compact interval. Apply the full entropy identity with terminal time \(t\in[a,b]\):

\[H(t)=H(a)+\int_a^t q(u)\,du.\]

An indefinite integral of an \(L^1\) function is absolutely continuous, and the Lebesgue differentiation theorem identifies its derivative almost everywhere. Thus

\[H\in AC([a,b]),\qquad H'(t)=q(t)\quad\text{for almost every }t\in(a,b).\]

The proof derives interval integrability from the raw-flux measurability and the verified majorant, then invokes absolute continuity and the almost-everywhere derivative of an integrable time primitive. This proves the required time regularity from the stated potential, log-Sobolev, and finite initial score-energy assumptions. A later score-pairing identity rewrites the raw Gaussian flux as negative Fisher energy plus the frozen gradient discrepancy, yielding the quantitative entropy-production estimate.

The flux is integrable on each positive compact interval, so the exact integrated identity makes entropy locally absolutely continuous there. Its derivative equals that flux almost everywhere, supplying the precise temporal regularity used in the final scalar proof.

sections.title: Averaging of the Gaussian component scores
sections.intro:
At positive time the Gaussian component score is \(S_{t,x}(y)=-(y-x+t abla U(x))/(2t)\). Differentiation of the mixture and positivity of \(p_t\) give \(p_t abla\log p_t=\int K_tS_{t,x}d\mu\). For a continuous field \(V\in L^2( ho_t)\), this identity may be paired with \(V\) and integrated.

Under the initial/output pair law, the component score has energy \(d/(2t)\), and \(V(y)\) has the same energy as under \( ho_t\). Cauchy–Schwarz therefore proves absolute integrability before Fubini is used. The resulting identity equates the kernel-weighted component-score pairing with the mixture-score pairing. Changing variables to \(Y_t=X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\) expresses the same pairing on the fixed independent initial/noise space used for entropy production.

steps.title: The score of one Gaussian component
steps.body:
For a fixed initial state \(x\), the Gaussian proposal has center \(c_t(x)=x-t\nabla U(x)\). Its score in the proposed state is \(S_{t,x}(y)=\nabla_y\log K_t(x,y)=-(y-c_t(x))/(2t)\). This definition is an explicit affine vector field. It is different from the mixture score, which averages this field over the posterior initial-state distribution.

Differentiate the logarithm of one Gaussian component in the observation variable. The normalizer is constant in that variable, leaving the negative centered displacement divided by \(2t\).

steps.title: Square-integrability of the component score
steps.body:
Represent the initial/output pair as \((X,Y_t)\), with \(Y_t=c_t(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\) and independent standard Gaussian \(Z\). Substituting into the component score cancels the center: \(S_{t,X}(Y_t)=-(\sqrt{2t}/(2t))Z\). The Gaussian identity random variable is square integrable; scalar multiplication and pullback to the product preserve this property. The map-measure theorem transfers it to the pair law. No initial position or gradient moment is needed for this component score.

Under the independent-noise representation the centered component displacement is \(\sqrt{2t}Z\). Its score energy is therefore \(d/(2t)\), finite for every positive time.

steps.title: Pulling a finite-energy state field to the pair space
steps.body:
If \(V\in L^2(\rho_t)\), then \(V(Y_t)\in L^2(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I))\), because \(\rho_t\) is the pushforward by the proposal. Map the independent pair to \((X,Y_t)\); a second application of the map-measure equivalence gives \((x,y)\mapsto V(y)\in L^2\) under the pair law. Continuity of \(V\) supplies the measurability required in both transfers.

A state-space field with finite square energy under \(\rho_t\) has the same square energy when composed with the proposed coordinate on the joint pair. This is pushforward change of variables.

steps.title: Integrability of the score-test pairing
steps.body:
The component score and the state field \(V(y)\) are both square integrable under the pair law. Holder's inequality makes the product of their norms integrable, and \(|\langle S,V\rangle|\le\|S\|\|V\|\) proves integrability of their inner product. The exact pair-density identity then rewrites this law as \(K_t(x,y)\mu(dx)dy\). The weighted-density equivalence gives joint integrability of \(K_t\langle S_{t,x},V(y)\rangle\) under \(\mu\otimes dy\), which is the hypothesis needed for Fubini in the averaging calculation.

Cauchy–Schwarz on the pair probability bounds the absolute pairing integral by the product of component-score and state-field \(L^2\) norms. Hence the signed pairing is integrable before its order is exchanged.

steps.title: The weighted mixture-score identity
steps.body:
The already constructed spatial derivative of the Gaussian mixture identifies its score as the posterior mean of the component score. The posterior density in \(x\) is \(K_t(x,y)/p_t(y)\), where \(p_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)>0\). Substitute this explicit weighted-density formula into the posterior integral and multiply by \(p_t(y)\). The common denominator cancels pointwise, giving \(p_t(y) abla\log p_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)S_{t,x}(y)d\mu(x)\). The precision and step-size forms have equal Gaussian normalizers, so this identity follows from the previously proved mixture derivative formula.

Integrating the component gradient over the starting law gives \( abla p_t\). Dividing by the positive mixture identifies its averaged score with \( abla\log p_t\), the posterior-score identity in weighted form.

steps.title: Integrability of the kernel-weighted score pairing
steps.body:
The component score is \(L^2\) under the pair probability law, hence is also \(L^1\). Identify that law with its explicit density \(K_t\) under \(\mu\otimes dy\). The vector-valued weighted-density integrability theorem gives \((x,y)\mapsto K_t(x,y)S_{t,x}(y)\in L^1(\mu\otimes dy)\). In particular, Fubini supplies integrability of the vector section in \(x\) for almost every output \(y\); this is needed before moving an inner product through its integral.

The Gaussian score has finite square norm and the tested state field has finite square norm. Their product is therefore integrable, supplying the precise Fubini hypothesis for the following averaging identity.

steps.title: Averaging the Gaussian component score
steps.body:
For almost every \(y\), vector-section integrability permits the linear functional \(w\mapsto\langle w,V(y)\rangle\) to commute with integration. The pointwise weighted-score identity then gives \(\int K_t(x,y)\langle S_{t,x}(y),V(y)\rangle d\mu(x)=p_t(y)\langle\nabla\log p_t(y),V(y)\rangle\).

The scalar pairing is jointly integrable by the preceding Holder argument, so Fubini exchanges the initial-state and output integrals. Integrate the displayed identity in \(y\). Finally \(p_t(y)dy=\rho_t(dy)\), with its explicit measurable finite density, changes the weighted Lebesgue integral into the integral under the interpolation law. Thus \(\int K_t\langle S_{t,x},V\rangle d\mu\,dy=\int\langle\nabla\log p_t,V\rangle d\rho_t\).

Average the component score at a fixed observation, then integrate its pairing with the state test. The mixture-gradient identity converts the result into the pairing with the Lebesgue score under \(\rho_t\).

steps.title: The score identity on the independent-noise space
steps.body:
Apply the measurable pair map \(T_t(x,z)=(x,Y_t(x,z))\) to the continuous pairing \(\langle S_{t,x}(y),V(y)\rangle\). The map-integral theorem expresses its pair-law integral as an integral over the fixed independent initial/noise space. The exact pair-density theorem expresses the same integral as the Gaussian-weighted Lebesgue pairing just evaluated.

Substitute \(Y_t=c_t(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\) in the component score. The residual becomes \(\sqrt{2t}z\), so the result is \(\mathbb E\langle-(\sqrt{2t}/(2t))Z,V(Y_t)\rangle=\mathbb E_{\rho_t}\langle\nabla\log p_t,V\rangle\). With \(V=\nabla\log r_t\), this identity turns the Gaussian-noise part of the raw entropy flux into the Lebesgue-score pairing needed for the full Fisher term.

Use the joint-law identity to rewrite the same integral on the original independent state-noise space. This lets the entropy flux be combined with the exact displacement and gradient-error estimates already proved there.

sections.title: Fisher dissipation and the Gaussian drift error
sections.intro:
The entropy chain rule gives a locally absolutely continuous entropy whose derivative is the Gaussian flux almost everywhere. The component-score averaging identity and the relative-score decomposition rewrite this flux as

\[Q_t=-I_t+\mathbb E\langle abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X), abla\log r_t(Y_t) angle.\]

All pairings are integrable by the square-energy estimates on the independent initial/noise space. Young's inequality bounds the error pairing by \(I_t/4\) plus its squared-gradient discrepancy. The latter is at most \(L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). Thus \(H'_t\le-3I_t/4+t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2\) almost everywhere at positive times. A countable family of positive compact intervals gives one full-measure time set on which the derivative conclusion holds, without a derivative assertion at zero.

steps.title: Justify inner-product integrability from two \(L^2\) fields
steps.body:
For vector fields \(F,G\in L^2(P)\), Hölder's inequality puts \(\|F\|\|G\|\) in \(L^1(P)\). Since \(|\langle F,G\rangle|\le\|F\|\|G\|\), their inner product is integrable.

The initial gradient, current gradient, Gaussian component score, and relative score all have the square energies proved above. Each needed pairing is therefore integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz. Their signed integrals may consequently be split and recombined in the entropy-flux algebra.

Cauchy–Schwarz proves absolute integrability of the pairing on the common independent-noise probability. This permits the exact entropy flux to be split into its Fisher and discrepancy contributions as ordinary integrals.

steps.title: The independent-noise score energy equals Fisher information
steps.body:
Let \(S_t(X,Z)= abla\log r_t(Y_t)\) and \(P=\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)\). The exact update-law identity gives

\[\mathbb E_P\|S_t\|^2=\int\| abla\log r_t\|^2\,d ho_t=I_t.\]

The state-space relative score square is integrable by the positive-time Fisher estimate. Change of variables through the measurable update preserves its integral. The jointly measurable field agrees pointwise with \( abla\log r_t\), and \(r_t u= ho_t\). Hence the transported integral equals the ordinary finite energy defining \(I_t\).

The composed relative score and the state-space relative score therefore have equal energy. Both use the representative constructed by Gaussian smoothing, so the identity concerns the same score as in the log-Sobolev inequality.

steps.title: Match the measurable state-space score field to the same finite Fisher value
steps.body:
The jointly measurable field used in time-space estimates agrees with the relative score at each positive time. Consequently

\[\int\|S_t(y)\|^2\,d\rho_t(y)=I_t.\]

The measurable state-space score equals the logarithmic gradient at positive time. Pushing its square energy through the proposal map preserves its integral. Thus this field, its independent-noise composition, and the score used in LSI all have the same finite Fisher energy.

At positive time the jointly measurable field equals the relative score pointwise. Its integrated energy therefore matches the finite Fisher quantity used in both LSI and production.

steps.title: The integrated Young inequality for the gradient discrepancy
steps.body:
Write \(D_t= abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\). The pointwise inequality

\[\langle D_t,S_t angle\le rac14\|S_t\|^2+\|D_t\|^2\]

is integrable because both squared norms have already been proved integrable. Their expectations satisfy \(\mathbb E\|S_t\|^2=I_t\) and

\[\mathbb E\|D_t\|^2\le L^2 igl(t^2G_0+2td igr),\qquad G_0=\mathbb E\| abla U(X)\|^2.\]

The discrepancy and score are measurable and square integrable by the preceding results. Cauchy–Schwarz makes their inner product integrable, so the pointwise Young inequality can be integrated as an ordinary inequality. Replace the score energy by \(I_t\) and insert the Gaussian discrepancy bound. The result is \(\mathbb E\langle D_t,S_t angle\le I_t/4+t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2\).

Apply \(\langle e,s angle\le\|e\|^2+\|s\|^2/4\) pointwise and integrate on the independent-noise space. The score energy becomes \(I_t/4\), while the error energy retains its sharp Gaussian bound.

steps.title: The entropy flux equals Fisher dissipation plus the gradient discrepancy
steps.body:
The raw entropy flux is \(-\mathbb E\langle g(X)-\sqrt{2t}Z/(2t),S_t angle\). The averaged Gaussian score identity gives

\[\mathbb E\left\langle- rac{\sqrt{2t}}{2t}Z,S_t ight angle=\int\langle abla\log p_t, abla\log r_t angle\,d ho_t.\]

Since \( abla\log r_t= abla U+ abla\log p_t\), the right side equals \(I_t-\mathbb E\langle abla U(Y_t),S_t angle\). Substituting and collecting the two gradient terms yields

\[Q_t=-I_t+\mathbb E\langle abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X),S_t angle.\]

The pulled-back initial gradient, current gradient, Gaussian component score, and relative score are all square integrable on the common probability space. Thus every inner product used in these sums and differences is integrable. Pushforward change of variables identifies the output-space pairings with these expectations. Applying the component-score averaging identity and then the relative-score decomposition justifies the two algebraic rearrangements. No separately chosen conditional drift is required.

Average the component Gaussian score using its established pairing identity. The flux then becomes \(-I_t+\mathbb E\langle abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X),S_t(Y_t) angle\), with no unproved conditional-drift choice.

steps.title: The entropy flux dissipation bound
steps.body:
Insert the integrated Young estimate into the exact entropy-flux decomposition:

\[Q_t=-I_t+\mathbb E\langle D_t,S_t\rangle\le-\frac34I_t+t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2.\]

The proof rewrites the flux with the decomposition of entropy flux into Fisher dissipation and the drift-discrepancy pairing, obtains the already justified numerical cross-term bound, and collects the scalar terms. The target's probability normalization and finite initial gradient energy suffice for this pointwise flux estimate. LSI is needed later to relate Fisher information to entropy, rather than to justify Young absorption.

Subtracting the absorbed quarter from the full negative Fisher term gives \(-3I_t/4\). The remaining discrepancy energy is at most \(t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2\), giving the desired scalar forcing.

steps.title: The positive-time entropy derivative inequality almost everywhere
steps.body:
The relative entropy is absolutely continuous on every compact interval inside \((0,\infty)\), and its derivative equals the raw flux almost everywhere there. To use this fact on an entire finite range \((0,T)\), choose the countable intervals

\[\left(\frac1{n+1},T+1\right),\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.\]

Intersect their full-measure derivative sets. Every \(t\in(0,T)\) belongs to at least one such interval because \(1/(n+1)\to0\). At that time the derivative equals the raw flux, so the pointwise flux bound gives

\[H'_t\le-\frac34 I_t+t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2\quad\text{for almost every }t\in(0,T).\]

Each interval has a full-measure set of times where the local entropy derivative equals the flux. Their countable intersection still has full measure. For any positive time outside this null set, choose \(n\) with \(1/(n+1)<t\); the local chain rule then applies at that time. Inserting the pointwise flux estimate proves the derivative inequality. The argument makes no assertion about a derivative at zero, where the initial law need not have a smooth density.

The local entropy identity supplies its derivative almost everywhere, and the pointwise flux bound holds at every positive time with finite energies. Intersecting these full-measure time conditions yields one almost-everywhere derivative inequality suitable for integration.

sections.title: The Gaussian density comparison near the initial time
sections.intro:
Assume the differentiable potential has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. For \(0<t<1/(4L)\), put \(\delta=1-4tL>0\) and \(s=t/\delta\). The smoothness inequalities compare the transition exponent weighted by Gibbs with a Gaussian exponent in the starting variable, centered at \(y-s abla U(y)\).

Completing the square leaves the term \(s\| abla U(y)\|^2/4\). Integration of the remaining Gaussian gives the normalizer ratio \((s/t)^{d/2}=\delta^{-d/2}\). Therefore the density of \( u P_t\) relative to \( u\) is at most \(\delta^{-d/2}\exp(s\| abla U(y)\|^2/4)\). This comparison supplies the reference-density correction in the initial entropy estimate, using only the stated differentiability and Lipschitz gradient assumptions.

steps.title: The Gaussian normalizer ratio
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), integration of the radial Gaussian gives \(N_t=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). Therefore for positive \(s,t\),

\[N_t/N_s=(s/t)^{d/2}.\]

The proof obtains the individual integrals from the finite-dimensional Gaussian integral, uses positivity to invert them, and applies the multiplication and division identities for real powers.

The normalizer scales as \(t^{-d/2}\), so replacing \(t\) by \(s=t/\delta\) contributes \((s/t)^{d/2}=\delta^{-d/2}\) when the reversed Gaussian is integrated. The direction of this ratio matters for the entropy correction's sign.

steps.title: Complete the square using only first derivatives
steps.body:
Write \(g_x=\nabla U(x)\), \(g_y=\nabla U(y)\), and choose positive \(s,t\) with \(s(1-4tL)=t\). The smooth upper model at \(y\) bounds \(U(y)-U(x)\) by \(\langle g_y,y-x\rangle+(L/2)\|y-x\|^2\). Lipschitzness gives \(\|g_x-g_y\|\le L\|x-y\|\). Expanding squares and bounding their cross term yields

\[U(y)-U(x)-\frac{\|y-x+tg_x\|^2}{4t}\le-\frac{\|x-y+sg_y\|^2}{4s}+\frac s4\|g_y\|^2.\]

The relation between \(s\) and \(t\) absorbs the Lipschitz error in the negative quadratic. Exponentiation preserves order. Multiplying by the positive Gaussian normalizer rewrites this as an upper bound on the Gibbs-weighted transition kernel.

Only the first-order smooth upper model and Lipschitz gradient comparison are used. Their quadratic terms are collected into the reversed Gaussian square, leaving the explicit positive correction in the observation-gradient norm.

steps.title: Integrate the comparison against the Gibbs start
steps.body:
The relative density of the updated Gibbs law is

\[r_{ u,t}(y)=\int N_t\exp\!\left(U(y)-U(x)- rac{\|y-x+t abla U(x)\|^2}{4t} ight)dx.\]

Insert the pointwise comparison. The remaining \(x\)-dependent expression is a normalized Gaussian with time \(s\) centered at \(y-s abla U(y)\), so its integral is one. The factors independent of \(x\) give

\[r_{ u,t}(y)\le(s/t)^{d/2}\exp\!\left( rac s4\| abla U(y)\|^2 ight).\]

Normalization of the original Gibbs probability cancels its partition function. Taking \(s=t/(1-4tL)\) later supplies an explicit reference-density bound whose logarithmic cost tends to zero.

After pointwise comparison, integrate the reversed Gaussian in the starting variable. Its total mass is one after its own normalizer is inserted, yielding the density-ratio upper bound needed at the initial entropy endpoint.

sections.title: Data processing and change of reference measure
sections.intro:
Apply the same Gaussian transition to the initial law \(\mu\) and the Gibbs law \( u\). Relative-entropy data processing gives \(H(\mu P_t\mid u P_t)\le H(\mu\mid u)\). To compare \(\mu P_t\) with \( u\), use the density bound for \( u P_t\) relative to \( u\).

The logarithmic likelihood through an intermediate reference is the sum of the two logarithmic likelihoods wherever their positive finite density ratios are defined. An integrable upper bound controls its positive part, and the exponential of the negative likelihood controls its negative part. This proves finite entropy against the new reference before the integrated comparison is used. The Gaussian reference-density bound is a constant plus a multiple of \(\| abla U\|^2\), and propagation of the gradient moment makes that correction integrable without an initial position moment.

steps.title: KL is unchanged by adjoining the same independent law
steps.body:
Adjoin the same independent probability innovation \(\eta\) to two finite measures. The log likelihood of \(\mu\otimes\eta\) relative to \(\nu\otimes\eta\) depends only on the first coordinate, so KL is unchanged. The proof uses the standard conditional-product KL identity with the constant Markov kernel \(x\mapsto\eta\); its conditional products are exactly the ordinary product measures. This equality supplies the independent-noise step in data processing.

Taking a product with the same independent probability does not change the likelihood ratio: it depends only on the first coordinate. Integrating out the extra factor therefore preserves the relative entropy.

steps.title: Adding log likelihoods through an intermediate law
steps.body:
For \(\mu\ll ho\ll u\), the Radon-Nikodym chain rule gives \(d\mu/d u=(d\mu/d ho)(d ho/d u)\) almost everywhere under the integrated law \(\mu\). Each factor is positive and finite there: positivity is transported along absolute continuity, and finiteness uses the probability measures' finite Radon-Nikodym derivatives.

On this full-measure set the density ratios are ordinary positive finite values, so the logarithm product rule applies. This proves \(\log(d\mu/d u)=\log(d\mu/d ho)+\log(d ho/d u)\), as an almost-everywhere identity under \(\mu\). The positivity and finiteness checks prevent using logarithm algebra at a zero or infinite density.

For three mutually compatible absolutely continuous laws, their density ratios multiply. Taking logarithms gives the sum of the two log likelihoods on the common full-measure set, before any integration is attempted.

steps.title: An exponential bound on the negative log likelihood
steps.body:
For \(\mu\ll u\), the reciprocal likelihood \(e^{-\log(d\mu/d u)}\) agrees \(\mu\)-almost everywhere with the real reverse Radon-Nikodym derivative \((d u/d\mu)\). This derivative is integrable under \(\mu\), even when \( u\) has a singular component relative to \(\mu\). Thus the negative exponential of the log likelihood is always integrable; finite KL has not been assumed at this stage.

The exponential of the negative log likelihood is a reciprocal density ratio. Its integral under the first law is bounded by the reference mass, giving control of the negative log-likelihood tail.

steps.title: Log-likelihood integrability from an upper bound
steps.body:
Suppose the log likelihood \(\ell=\log(d\mu/d\nu)\) has an integrable upper bound \(b\). Where \(\ell\ge0\), \(|\ell|\le b\le|b|\). Where \(\ell<0\), the elementary exponential bound gives \(|\ell|=-\ell\le e^{-\ell}\). Hence globally \(|\ell|\le|b|+e^{-\ell}\). The first term is integrable by hypothesis, and the second by reciprocal-likelihood integrability. Measurable domination proves \(\ell\in L^1(\mu)\), controlling its negative tail without a lower density bound.

An integrable upper bound controls the positive part, while the exponential estimate controls the negative part. Together they establish absolute integrability of the log likelihood needed for the entropy chain rule.

steps.title: Entropy comparison through a reference density bound
steps.body:
Assume finite \(H(\mu\mid ho)\), \( ho\ll u\), and \(d ho/d u\le e^b\), with \(b\in L^1(\mu)\). Finite KL gives \(\mu\ll ho\), hence \(\mu\ll u\). The density bound transfers to \(\mu\)-almost every point, where positivity of the intermediate density permits logarithms. Thus \(\log(d ho/d u)\le b\).

The log-likelihood chain rule gives \(\log(d\mu/d u)\le\log(d\mu/d ho)+b\). Its right side is integrable. The preceding one-sided integrability theorem therefore proves the new log likelihood integrable and hence \(H(\mu\mid u)<\infty\). Only after proving finiteness do we integrate the inequality, yielding \(H(\mu\mid u)\le H(\mu\mid ho)+\mathbb E_\mu b\). Finite entropy against the new reference is a conclusion, rather than an additional premise.

Decompose the log likelihood through the intermediate reference law. Its first entropy is controlled by data processing, and the density-ratio upper bound controls the added term by an integrable observable.

steps.title: Data processing for the Gaussian transition
steps.body:
The interpolation is the measurable image of the initial law times standard Gaussian noise under \((x,z)\mapsto x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\). Apply KL data processing to this same map for both initial laws. The independent-noise product identity removes the common Gaussian factor, giving \(H( ho_t^\mu\mid ho_t^ u)\le H(\mu\mid u)\). This argument compares two evolved laws and does not assert that either law is invariant under the discrete step.

Both inputs are passed through the same measurable Gaussian update with the same independent noise law. Relative-entropy data processing therefore bounds the two output laws by the divergence of their inputs.

steps.title: Propagation of the gradient moment
steps.body:
Write \( abla U(Y_t)=[ abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)]+ abla U(X)\). The initial gradient is \(L^2\), and the frozen-error energy theorem makes the bracketed discrepancy \(L^2\) on the independent initial/noise space. Their sum is \(L^2\); the map-measure equivalence transfers this to the interpolation law.

Pointwise, the squared norm of the sum is at most twice each squared norm. Integrate and insert \(\mathbb E\| abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). The initial-coordinate marginal gives the remaining \(G_0\), so \(G_t\le2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2\). This proves both integrability and the quantitative estimate without a position moment.

Lipschitzness bounds \(\| abla U(Y_t)\|^2\) by \(2\| abla U(X)\|^2+2L^2\|Y_t-X\|^2\). The exact displacement moment then yields the displayed propagated energy.

steps.title: The interpolation entropy upper bound
steps.body:
Let \( ho_t\) be the evolved input and \(\sigma_t\) the evolved Gibbs target. Data processing gives \(H( ho_t\mid\sigma_t)\le H_0<\infty\). Suppose the reference law satisfies \(d\sigma_t/d u\le\exp(b+c\| abla U\|^2)\), with its absolute continuity retained explicitly.

Finite initial KL first supplies finite \(G_0\) through the direct entropy/score estimate. The propagated gradient-moment theorem then proves \(G_t<\infty\). Consequently the logarithmic reference correction \(b+c\| abla U\|^2\) is integrable under \( ho_t\). Apply the finite-entropy change-of-reference theorem to obtain \(H( ho_t\mid u)<\infty\) and \(H( ho_t\mid u)\le H_0+b+cG_t\). The preceding Gibbs comparison establishes the pointwise reference-density bound.

Insert the explicit log density-ratio bound and the propagated gradient moment into the entropy decomposition. This gives a finite upper bound on interpolation entropy, suitable for sending elapsed time to zero.

sections.title: An entropy upper bound at the initial time
sections.intro:
Let \(H_0<\infty\) be the initial relative entropy and \(G_0=\int\|\nabla U\|^2d\mu\), finite by the preceding entropy-moment estimate. With \(\delta(t)=1-4tL\), define

\[B(t)=H_0-\frac d2\log\delta(t)+\frac{t}{4\delta(t)}\left[2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2\right].\]

The updated Gibbs density comparison, data processing, and propagated gradient bound give finite interpolation entropy \(H_t\le B(t)\) for sufficiently small positive \(t\). The denominator tends to one, so \(B\) is continuous at zero and \(B(0)=H_0\). This upper bound supplies the initial value in the scalar comparison. No initial Fisher information, position second moment, or continuity assumption on the entropy path at zero is needed.

steps.title: The explicit initial-endpoint majorant
steps.body:
Put \(\delta(t)=1-4tL\) and \(G_0=\mathbb E_\mu\|\nabla U\|^2\). Define the explicit upper bound \(B(t)=H_0-\frac d2\log\delta(t)+\frac{t}{4\delta(t)}[2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2]\). The logarithmic term is the normalizer correction from the updated Gibbs density; the final term uses the propagated gradient moment. The definition is a scalar function at all times, while its entropy interpretation below requires \(t>0\) and \(\delta(t)>0\).

The majorant combines the data-processing entropy with the Gaussian normalizer correction and a gradient-energy correction. Its explicit denominator is positive for all sufficiently small positive times, so the expression is an ordinary finite scalar there.

steps.title: The majorant at zero
steps.body:
At \(t=0\), the logarithm has argument \(\delta(0)=1\), hence is zero. The coefficient \(t/(4\delta(t))\) is zero as well. Both correction terms vanish exactly, proving \(B(0)=H_0\). This is a direct algebraic evaluation of the constructed scalar function. No limit of the entropy path is assumed.

At zero the logarithmic term is \(\log1=0\), and the entire energy correction has a factor \(t\). Hence the value is precisely the initial entropy, even when the initial law has no smooth density.

steps.title: Continuity of the majorant at zero
steps.body:
The denominator \(\delta(t)\) has value one at zero, so it stays nonzero locally. The logarithm is continuous at that same positive value. All other terms in \(B\) are polynomial or constant scalar operations. Their continuity proves \(B(t)\to B(0)=H_0\) as \(t\to0\). The initial gradient integral is an already defined scalar; its finiteness in the entropy application is established by the finite-KL moment theorem.

The denominator tends to one and is nonzero near zero. Continuity of the logarithm at one, polynomial factors, and reciprocal then proves continuity of the full majorant at the endpoint.

steps.title: The interpolation entropy lies below the upper bound
steps.body:
For positive \(t\) with \(\delta=1-4tL>0\), choose the comparison Gaussian time \(s=t/\delta\). The updated Gibbs law has an explicit relative density bounded by \((s/t)^{d/2}\exp(s\|\nabla U(y)\|^2/4)\). Since \(s/t=\delta^{-1}\), this is \(\exp[-(d/2)\log\delta+(s/4)\|\nabla U(y)\|^2]\).

The relative density identifies the Radon-Nikodym derivative and proves absolute continuity of the updated Gibbs reference law. The change-of-reference entropy estimate then gives finite \(H_t\) and \(H_t\le H_0-(d/2)\log\delta+(s/4)G_t\). The coefficient \(s/4\) is nonnegative, so inserting \(G_t\le2(1+L^2t^2)G_0+4tdL^2\) proves \(H_t\le B(t)\).

The density-ratio comparison bounds output entropy by the majorant whenever \(1-4tL>0\). The finite score moment supplies all integrability required for the likelihood decomposition.

steps.title: The entropy majorant on a positive neighborhood
steps.body:
For all sufficiently small positive \(t\), specifically \(t<1/(8L)\), one has \(1-4tL>0\). The previous positive-time entropy bound therefore applies eventually in the right neighborhood of zero, giving \(H_t\le B(t)\). Combined with continuity of \(B\) and \(B(0)=H_0\), this supplies the upper initial boundary used in scalar comparison. It does not insert an assumption that \(H_t\) is differentiable or continuous at zero.

A sufficiently small positive neighborhood satisfies the denominator condition. Thus the entropy upper bound is available along every approach to zero through positive times, exactly the endpoint control used in scalar comparison.

sections.title: Integration of almost-everywhere entropy dissipation
sections.intro:
Suppose the entropy is locally absolutely continuous on positive-time compact intervals and satisfies an affine differential inequality almost everywhere. Multiplication by the exponential integrating factor and the fundamental theorem of calculus give the corresponding affine comparison on each such interval.

At the lower endpoint use an explicit upper bound \(H(s)\le M(s)\), where \(M\) is continuous at zero. Sending \(s\downarrow0\) gives the comparison with \(M(0)\), without requiring continuity or differentiability of \(H\) at zero. Applying this argument to the Fisher dissipation and gradient-moment estimates, then using the stated step restriction, proves the one-step bound with forcing \(6h^2dL^2\).

steps.title: Integrate the affine differential inequality
steps.body:
Suppose \(H\) is absolutely continuous on \([s,t]\) and \(H^{\prime}\le-aH+b\) almost everywhere, with \(a>0\). Set \(F(u)=e^{au}(H(u)-b/a)\). Products of absolutely continuous functions on a compact interval are absolutely continuous. The product rule holds almost everywhere and gives \(F^{\prime}(u)=e^{au}(a(H(u)-b/a)+H^{\prime}(u))\le0\).

The fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions gives \(F(t)-F(s)=\int_s^tF^{\prime}\le0\). Multiply by \(e^{-at}>0\), cancel the exponentials, and rearrange:

\[H(t)\le e^{-a(t-s)}H(s)+\frac ba(1-e^{-a(t-s)}).\]

The proof removes no exceptional set by assuming a derivative there; both differentiability and the inequality are used only almost everywhere.

Local absolute continuity gives an integrable derivative and the fundamental theorem on each positive compact interval. Multiplying by the smooth integrating factor preserves absolute continuity, so integrating its almost-everywhere derivative bound is legitimate.

steps.title: Send the positive initial time to zero
steps.body:
Suppose \(H\) is absolutely continuous on every \([s,T]\), \(0<s<T\), and \(H(s)\le M(s)\) for all sufficiently small positive \(s\). If \(M\) is continuous at zero, the preceding estimate gives

\[H(T)\le e^{-a(T-s)}M(s)+\frac ba(1-e^{-a(T-s)}).\]

The right side tends to \(e^{-aT}M(0)+(b/a)(1-e^{-aT})\). Order is preserved under limits, giving the desired initial-endpoint bound. Single endpoints have zero Lebesgue measure, so an inequality on the open interval suffices. Continuity or differentiability of \(H\) at zero is not needed.

The upper initial majorant converges to the finite initial entropy. Applying it at the lower positive endpoint and sending that endpoint to zero therefore bounds the limiting comparison term from above, which is all the scalar inequality requires.

steps.title: Absorb the ULA forcing with its exact constants
steps.body:
Assume \(2\alpha H\le I\), \(H^{\prime}\le-3I/4+t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2\), and \(G_0\le4L^2M(0)/\alpha+2dL\). Let \(0<h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\), \(0<\alpha\le L\), and \(M(0)\ge0\). Then \(hL\le1/4\), \(\alpha h\le1/4\),

\[h^2L^2(4L^2/\alpha)\le\alpha/4,\qquad h^2L^2(2dL)\le hdL^2/2.\]

The derivative is therefore at most \(-3\alpha H/2+B\), where \(B=\alpha M(0)/4+(5/2)hdL^2\). The affine comparison and \(1-e^{-ah}\le ah\) imply \(H(h)\le e^{-3\alpha h/2}M(0)+Bh\). Finally \(e^{-x}\ge e^{-3x/2}+x/4\) for \(0\le x\le1/4\) absorbs the entropy part of \(Bh\). Bounding \(5/2\) by 6 gives

\[H(h)\le e^{-\alpha h}M(0)+6h^2dL^2.\]

The probability-law convergence theorem supplies each of these analytic hypotheses before applying this scalar estimate.

The time-dependent forcing is first bounded uniformly using \(t\le h\). The initial-entropy contribution is absorbed by the exponential gap, while the dimensional forcing integrates to a multiple of \(h^2dL^2\), giving the stated one-step coefficient.

sections.title: The entropy bound for the Gaussian ULA laws
sections.intro:
Let \(U\) be differentiable with globally \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and suppose its normalized Gibbs probability satisfies the stated log-Sobolev inequality with \(\alpha>0\). Let the initial probability have finite relative entropy. For \(0<h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\), the Gaussian ULA iterates have finite relative entropy and satisfy

\[H(\rho_k\mid\nu)\le e^{-\alpha hk}H(\rho_0\mid\nu)+\frac{8hdL^2}{\alpha}.\]

Finite current entropy gives its gradient second moment. Positive-time Gaussian smoothing gives positive \(C^1\) relative densities and finite Fisher information, and the log-Sobolev inequality gives finite next entropy. The integrated entropy identity, the initial entropy upper bound, and \(\alpha\le L\) then yield the one-step recurrence. Induction and geometric summation prove the estimate. In dimension zero, all probability laws agree and their relative entropy is zero.

steps.title: Handle the singleton state space and a zero smoothness parameter
steps.body:
On a singleton state space every probability measure is equal: any measurable set either contains the unique point and is the whole space, or is empty. Measure extensionality and probability normalization therefore identify any two laws. In particular their KL divergence is zero.

For the substantive entropy calculation one works with \(L>0\), so that the step restriction and exponential score moment have their usual positive denominators. In positive dimension, \(\alpha\le L\) and \(\alpha>0\) guarantee this positivity. The singleton case has already been resolved directly with zero KL, so it needs no division by a smoothness constant.

When the state space is a singleton, every probability law is the same point mass and KL is zero. In the nondegenerate case, the compatibility argument rules out zero smoothness when the LSI constant is positive, permitting the subsequent divisions by \(L\).

steps.title: Finiteness of entropy at every ULA iterate
steps.body:
Start from the supplied finite initial KL and induct on \(k\). If \(\rho_k\) has finite KL, the direct entropy/score estimate gives \(\nabla U\in L^2(\rho_k)\). For the positive-time Gaussian interpolation, the Lebesgue score energy is at most \(d/(2h)\), and the propagated gradient moment is finite. Thus relative Fisher information is finite. LSI with \(\alpha>0\) then gives finite KL of the output.

The endpoint law is exactly \(\rho_{k+1}\), so this proves the finite-entropy induction step. The finiteness conclusion needs only positivity of the step; its smaller quantitative restriction is used later for contraction and forcing absorption.

The induction begins with the assumed finite initial KL. Finite current KL supplies its score moment; the positive-time Gaussian transition has finite Fisher energy; LSI then gives finite next KL. Thus each entropy term is finite before the recurrence is iterated.

steps.title: Derive all scalar step restrictions
steps.body:
In positive dimension, the bounded sinusoidal tests in compatibility give \(\alpha\le L\). Since \(\alpha>0\), also \(L>0\). Multiplying the original restriction by \(4L^2>0\) gives \(4hL^2\le\alpha\le L\), hence \(hL\le1/4\). Multiplying \(\alpha\le L\) by \(h>0\) also gives \(\alpha h\le1/4\).

The final theorem splits off the singleton case before invoking this positive-dimensional argument. No separate compatibility assumption is required.

From \(h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\) and \(\alpha\le L\), derive \(hL\le1/4\) and \(\alpha h\le1/4\). These numerical consequences are checked before invoking the scalar absorption and geometric-denominator lemmas.

steps.title: The log-Sobolev inequality for the positive-time density
steps.body:
Finite initial KL supplies the initial gradient moment. The Gaussian mixture is positive \(C^1\) relative to Gibbs, has finite KL, and has finite Fisher information at every \(t>0\). Apply the original extended-valued LSI to this density. Since both sides are finite, order is preserved on passing to their real values:

\[2\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}( ho_t\mid u)\le I_t.\]

The integral form identifies \(I_t\) with \(\int\|\mathcal S(t,y)\|^2d ho_t(y)\), using the proved equality between the measurable score field and \( abla\log r_t\), and the equality \(r_t u= ho_t\). The second version keeps the extended-Fisher notation for the entropy-production assembly.

At positive elapsed time, the constructed relative density is positive, \(C^1\), and normalized, with finite Fisher and KL. It therefore belongs to the original LSI test class, giving \(2\alpha H(t)\le I_t\) for the interpolation law.

steps.title: The analytic hypotheses of the one-step scalar comparison
steps.body:
Fix any finite-KL probability law \(\mu\). The score-exponential argument gives the integrability of \(\| abla U\|^2\) and

\[G_0\le4L^2H_ u(\mu)/\alpha+2dL.\]

The bounded-log entropy identity proves local absolute continuity of the interpolation entropy \(H(t)\) on every \([s,h]\) with \(s>0\). The Gaussian weak equation and Young estimate give \(H^{\prime}\le-3I/4+t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2\) almost everywhere. The preceding LSI estimate supplies \(2\alpha H\le I\).

The explicit initial majorant \(M\) is continuous at zero, satisfies \(M(0)=H_ u(\mu)\), and bounds \(H(t)\) for sufficiently small positive \(t\). These are exactly the premises of the integrating-factor comparison for a locally absolutely continuous entropy curve, giving

\[H_ u(\mu P_h)\le e^{-\alpha h}H_ u(\mu)+6h^2dL^2.\]

The singleton case instead uses equality of probability laws and nonnegativity of the right side. The density, weak equation, entropy regularity, and moment estimates used here follow from the stated potential, log-Sobolev, and finite initial entropy assumptions.

The entropy curve has local absolute continuity, the almost-everywhere production bound, and an upper initial majorant continuous at zero. Together with the entropy-derived score moment, these supply every premise of the scalar one-step comparison.

steps.title: The discrete relative-entropy recurrence
steps.body:
The law \(\rho_k\) is a probability measure by the proved Gaussian Markov construction. Its KL is finite by the induction above. Apply the single-transition estimate with \(\mu=\rho_k\). The interpolation endpoint is precisely \(\rho_{k+1}\), yielding

\[H_{k+1}\le e^{-\alpha h}H_k+6h^2dL^2.\]

Here \(H_k=H(\rho_k\mid\nu)\), a finite real number by the preceding induction, and \(\rho_k\) is the \(k\)-fold Gaussian transition applied to the initial probability. The one-step comparison therefore yields a recurrence for the entropies of these specified probability laws.

Use the exact interpolation endpoints to replace the scalar initial and final entropies by \(H_k\) and \(H_{k+1}\). The comparison then gives \(H_{k+1}\le e^{-\alpha h}H_k+6h^2dL^2\) without any separately assumed recurrence.

steps.title: Sum the recurrence and retain the finite-KL guard
steps.body:
Retain the output-entropy finiteness already proved. In positive dimension, the step estimates give \(\alpha h\le1/4\). The scalar geometric-sum theorem applied to the recurrence gives

\[H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+\frac{6h^2dL^2}{1-e^{-\alpha h}}\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+\frac{8hdL^2}{\alpha}.\]

The final inequality uses \(1-e^{-x}\ge3x/4\) for \(0\le x\le1/4\). In dimension zero, equality of probability measures makes the left side zero and the result follows by nonnegativity.

The final hypotheses are differentiability, globally Lipschitz gradient, the Gibbs LSI with positive constant, a positive admissible step, and finite initial KL. Probability normalization of the target is included in LSI. Every density, moment, weak-equation, and entropy-regularity property used in the recurrence has been derived above from these assumptions.

Apply the geometric recurrence estimate to the finite sequence of relative entropies. The positive denominator bound converts the forcing sum into \(8hdL^2/\alpha\), yielding the final statement under only the displayed potential, LSI, step, and initial-entropy assumptions.

sections.title: Comparison of the proof with the source argument
sections.intro: The source and present conclusions agree on the Gaussian transition, LSI normalization, step restriction, entropy rate, and coefficients \(6\) and \(8\). The proof below derives its density, moment, and entropy-regularity estimates from the original assumptions. Several intermediate proof choices differ from the paper and are recorded explicitly in the comparison below.

steps.title: Corresponding estimates in the source proof
steps.body:
The full paper, Appendix B.2.1, proves the one-step result; Appendix B.2.2 iterates it. The Gaussian update, displacement energy, Young coefficient \(-3/4\), one-step coefficient \(6\), and final coefficient \(8\) agree with that argument.

The present proof obtains the needed gradient moment directly from a Gaussian-averaged score MGF and the entropy variational inequality, avoiding an LSI-to-Talagrand step. It derives \(\alpha\le L\) using bounded tests and integration by parts. It justifies the entropy equation with bounded smooth log primitives, spacetime \(L^1\) differentiation and dominated limits, then treats time zero through a proved continuous entropy upper envelope.

The scalar comparison uses exact affine comparison and an exponential-gap estimate, with intermediate coefficient \(5/2\) before relaxing it to \(6\). This is a proof variation with the same final assumptions and conclusion.

steps.title: Positive-time entropy calculus and the initial-time upper bound
steps.body:
The density hypotheses stated earlier give one sufficient condition for dominated differentiation. The Gaussian argument does not require these stronger data on a closed interval containing zero. Spatial differentiation of the Gaussian mixture gives a positive \(C^1\) relative density with finite Fisher information. Time differentiation gives its local space-time \(L^1\) derivative bound. Bounded logarithmic primitives and dominated convergence then prove local absolute continuity and the almost-everywhere derivative of relative entropy at positive times.

At the initial time, the entropy comparison proves \(H(t)\le M(t)\) with \(M\) continuous at zero and \(M(0)=H(0)\), by data processing and a pointwise bound on the evolved Gibbs density. The integrated differential inequality then permits the positive starting time to tend to zero using this upper bound. No initial smooth density, initial Fisher information, entropy continuity premise, or potential smoothing limit is required.

steps.title: The joint gradient discrepancy in entropy production
steps.body:
Conditional expectation gives a measurable error field with the required energy and flux identities. Alternatively, the joint initial-state and Gaussian-noise variables give the same pairing directly. Differentiating the kernel and applying integration by parts proves the weak equation for bounded \(C^1\) tests with finite gradient energy. Averaging the component score identifies it with the mixture score, so the entropy derivative is

\[H'(t)=-I(t)+\mathbb E\langle\nabla U(Y_t)-\nabla U(X),S_t(Y_t)\rangle.\]

The joint error has proved energy at most \(L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). Young's inequality gives \(H'\le-3I/4+L^2(t^2G_0+2td)\). The bounded-log limit is justified by spacetime Fisher and Gaussian velocity energies, so no unbounded entropy test is silently assumed admissible.

steps.title: The gradient moment and the relation between the two constants
steps.body:
Translation invariance and the smooth upper model imply a sub-Gaussian score MGF under the Gibbs target. Gaussian averaging gives

\[\int e^{\| abla U\|^2/(4L)}d u\le2^{d/2}\le e^{d/2}.\]

The entropy variational inequality proves score integrability and

\[G_\mu\le4L H_ u(\mu)+2dL\le(4L^2/\alpha)H_ u(\mu)+2dL.\]

Compatibility \(\alpha\le L\) is proved in positive dimension from LSI applied to normalized exponentials of bounded \(C^1\) functions, a bounded-test variance bound, the Gibbs score integration-by-parts identity, and bounded sinusoidal tests converging to the unit direction. Dimension zero is handled by uniqueness of the probability law. The original positive \(C^1\) LSI test class suffices because all exponential and Gaussian relative-density tests are proved admissible. Thus the final theorem assumes no entropy-cost coupling, additional compatibility inequality, or gradient-moment estimate.

closing:
The Gaussian ULA laws therefore satisfy the entropy estimate from the target log-Sobolev inequality, first-order smoothness, the step restriction, and finite initial relative entropy. The proof derives the required gradient moment, positive-time density and Fisher bounds, the entropy-production inequality, and the initial-time upper bound. Scalar integration gives the one-step coefficient \(6\), and the geometric recurrence gives the final coefficient \(8\).

The intermediate conditional results retain their analytic hypotheses and can be applied to other identified interpolation laws. The displayed source statements record the exact assumptions and conclusions corresponding to each mathematical argument.
